Thank you, my Lord. There's also the issue of discharging the supplemental jurors that we'll need to deal with.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Home straight now as far as I'm concerned, at least -- or listening to me is concerned.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can I just deal with a mistake that I made yesterday. I was giving you my layman's description of the epiglottis and, predictably, I got it wrong. The epiglottis is actually a flap of tissue that sits beneath the tongue at the back of the throat and its main function is to close over the windpipe when you swallow so food or liquids don't go into your lungs. So sorry about that.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We are going to move back to the indictment, please, and the case of [Baby P]. It's count 21. At the end of yesterday I told you that his brother, [Baby O], had been murdered by Lucy Letby on 23 June. You will see on page 8 of the indictment [Baby P]’s name appearing.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We allege that Lucy Letby murdered [Baby P] on the following day, on the 24th.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So I'm going to start, so far as [Baby P] is concerned, with what happened from his perspective on the day we say Lucy Letby murdered his brother, so 23 June. Do you remember, by that stage, this was day 3 for him, having been born on 21 June?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby P] was breathing for himself on the 23rd in air, so no supplemental oxygen required, from 6.30 on the morning of the 23rd. And as I've already told you, I'll just remind you, he was in room number 2 with his brother, [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby fed [Baby P] some donor expressed breast milk on the day shift at 8 am, 10 am, noon, 2 pm and 6 pm. The final feed, the one at 6 pm, which you know is an hour and a half or so, up to 2 hours before the end of the shift, Lucy Letby recorded at 6. If it was accurately recorded, the time of it was accurately recorded, it was at about 13 minutes after [Baby O] had died.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There was no record of anything unusual happening with [Baby P], either before or after he was fed. I'm just going to show you the feeding chart now if, I may. It's page 23981.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm sure you're already reasonably familiar with how these things work, but I'll just remind you, if I may.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the top left-hand corner, [Baby P]’s name appears. His date of birth underneath. In the top right-hand corner, day 3, in other words -- you remember the day of birth is counted as day 1.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You can see when the NGT, the nasogastric tube, was due to be changed, there's the length of the tube from mouth to stomach, 19 centimetres, and you can see where it was and the tube inserted was on the 23rd -- I think it says "right" -- and then "20", so maybe that's 20 centimetres.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Underneath there we have the feeding chart itself.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay? If you go down -- if we go down the chart to where it says "Feeds", which is -- thank you. Perfect.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What we can see is that -- and if you look right down to the bottom of the page you can see initials at the bottom of the page and the signature line at the very bottom.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There are two sets of initials in some of these cases. RM and LL. Lucy Letby, obviously, is LL. RM is the student nurse I told you about yesterday, Rebecca Morgan.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So you can see immediately that [Baby P] was being fed every 2 hours. He was being fed at the beginning of the shift at 8 o'clock, 13 millilitres, you can see. Then when you get on to 2 pm you can see the amount of feed was increased to 15 millilitres, and above where it says "15" you can see "NG", which is route, so nasogastric tube rather than a bottle, and above that you can see "EBM", which means expressed breast milk. And you can see -- underneath the 15, you can see what in effect is a running total for the day. Okay?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So up to and including the feed at 12 o'clock, [Baby P] that day had had 76 millilitres, plus the 15 given at 14.00 hours, which gives you the running total of 91 and so on.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So just going back to the bottom line again, the signature line, as I said, Rebecca Morgan and Lucy Letby. But you can see that the 6 o'clock feed, so the last feed of the day shift, is Lucy Letby alone, so no Rebecca Morgan countersignature.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we now go, just to make this page look more complicated, to just below the feed box that's now in orange, there's another line saying "Aspirates". What I'm going to concentrate on, ladies and gentlemen, is the aspirates during the day shift, so 8 o'clock onwards.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do you remember what an aspirate is? I'm sure.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I keep repeating this because in the context of this case it's important. It's the amount drawn up with a syringe through the nasogastric tube from the stomach.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So it's checking whether there's anything in the stomach before the baby was fed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What you can see in handwriting is, at 8 o'clock, trace. 10 o'clock, trace. Midday, I think it's a small vomit. 2 pm, trace. 4 pm, trace. And nothing at all written in there on the occasion that Lucy Letby was doing this alone.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And yet when we get to the first feed of the night shift, so almost at the moment that Lucy Letby handed over [Baby P] to the night shift nurse, when the night shift nurse drew the aspirate, the night shift nurse retrieved 14 millilitres of milk, which is
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: 1 millilitre short of what, if the chart is the truth as to what Lucy Letby withdrew, it's all but 1 millilitre of what [Baby P] had been fed 2 hours earlier.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because [Baby O] had died in such unusual circumstances, [Baby P] was reviewed by the consultant, Dr Gibbs, at 6 pm, and Dr Gibbs recorded that [Baby P]’s abdomen was full and mildly distended. There was no tenderness, he had active bowel sounds, which is a good sign, as is the lack of tenderness of his abdomen.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was screened for infection. An X-ray taken at 8 o'clock, so the time that that 14-millilitre aspirate was removed from [Baby P]’s stomach, showed a striking gaseous distension, a swelling caused by gas throughout his stomach and his whole bowel.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Undoubtedly that was at a time when Lucy Letby was still on the ward because the electronic note that she made, which is timed automatically by the computer, is timed at 8.24. Putting it bluntly, ladies and gentlemen, the allegation here is that she deliberately caused a problem for [Baby P] as she was going off duty so that overnight he'd have problems, which would divert attention away from Lucy Letby. So that's the allegation. I'm sure you've seen that coming, but that's the allegation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Anyway, on the night shift, the milk feeds were stopped for [Baby P] because another large part-digested aspirate was drawn up the nasogastric tube at feeding time.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And during the night shift [Baby P]’s abdomen was full but soft. So full, a warning sign; soft, a good sign.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: However, by 6.39 the following morning, the night shift nurse, who was Sophie Ellis, recorded in the notes that:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Abdo has been soft and non-distended..."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So the abdomen had gone back to normal and was soft, that 25 millilitres of air had been aspirated by one of the nurses and that the nasogastric tube had been put on free drainage, which you'll remember means any excess air can vent, so it doesn't cause a problem.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So, ladies and gentlemen, it looks from the records that the problem that Lucy Letby handed over [Baby P] with to Sophie Ellis had been resolved by the end of the night shift and it seems that the problem, or one of the problems, was too much air in [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The next medical note, in other words the next doctor's note, was made on the 24th, so the day [Baby P] was to die, at 9.35 in
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: the morning. But before that, when the day shift came on at 7.30/8.00, Lucy Letby had been designated as [Baby P]’s nurse again. [Baby P] was still in room 2, this time he was with his brother, [Baby R], so the third triplet, and also [Baby R]’s designated nurse was Lucy Letby. But as events unfolded with [Baby P], Christopher Booth became [Baby R]’s designated nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On this day shift the other nurses were [Nurse D], Yvonne Farmer and the student Rebecca Morgan, Janet Cox and Angela McShane were the nursery nurses, so there had been a couple of changes in personnel again from the day before.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Text messages that Lucy Letby sent to [Dr A], just after 8.30 that morning, so about an hour after she'd arrived at work, suggest that she had sent or was sending the student Rebecca Morgan with a baby who was leaving the unit to go for an MRI scan, a magnetic resonance imaging scan.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Another registrar, Dr Ukoh, recorded that at 9.35, so this is the first medical note of the shift, [Baby P] was selfventilating in air, that he had desaturated plus, and had had a bradycardia, which means his heart rate was decreased, that he had a moderately distended bloated abdomen and a slightly mottled skin. So this is an hour and a half or so after Lucy Letby took over again.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the nursing notes, and I'll show you these, which were made by Lucy Letby, she recorded this -- and it's the bit that's highlighted, ladies and gentlemen, you can see that these are made much later in the day.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: These are made after the end of the day shift between 21.28 and 22.00 hours, so that evening.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You can see above the highlighted part it says:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Written in retrospect [this is a reference to the notes themselves] for care given from 8 in the morning."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then the standard checks are set out. You'll see this sort of entry in pretty much every example of the nursing notes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Moving on to the highlighted part:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "NG tube on free drainage. Trace amount in tube. Abdomen full. Loops visible."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's a reference to the loops of bowel, so literally the loops visible through the skin. That's the suggestion:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Soft to touch. Registrar Ukoh arrived to carry out ward round. [Baby P] had an apnoea..."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So breathing problems:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "... brady [bradycardia, reduced heart rate], desaturation [reduced oxygen saturations] with mottled appearance, requiring facial oxygen and Neopuff for approximately 1 minute. Abdomen becoming distended. Decision made to carry out bloods and gas, approximately 09.30."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So what we see here, ladies and gentlemen, the reason I started with the day before, is the day before [Baby P] had been fine, no problem.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At the moment he was handed over to another nurse, all of a sudden [Baby P] had a problem. Overnight, the other nurse resolved the problem and yet within an hour and a half or 2 hours of the reappearance of Lucy Letby, the problem reappeared.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Fifteen minutes later, [Baby P] suffered an acute desaturation, a crash call went out, and [Dr B] and Doctor Ukoh, [Dr A] and Cooke attended. On their arrival, [Baby P]’s heart rate was about 80 beats a minute, his saturations were down to 60%, and he had to be intubated, so the ET tube had to be put down his throat and that improved him. Efforts were then made to transfer [Baby P] to the more specialist hospital at Arrowe Park.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: While those efforts to relocate [Baby P] were going on, [Baby P] desaturated again at 11.30. This time he was given adrenaline and he was paralysed with a drug which would have helped the ventilation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Due to the treatment, his spontaneous circulation was restored, but he continued to deteriorate through the day. And at 12.30, a punctured lung, a pneumothorax, was identified from an X-ray that had been taken about 33 minutes earlier and the treatment for that started 10 minutes after it had been identified in the X-ray.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 3 pm the transport team from Arrowe Park arrived and just before they arrived, [Baby P]’s blood gases had been taken and were satisfactory. [Dr B], who was supervising [Baby P]’s treatment and was optimistic for his prospects. All of a sudden Lucy Letby said to him, Lucy Letby said to [Dr B], something like, "He's not leaving here alive, is he?", an echo of what she had said when [Baby C] collapsed. Do you remember?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That remark surprised [Dr B], but Lucy Letby's prediction came true. After all, she knew what she had done to [Baby P] and therefore she knew what was likely to happen. And it was
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: certainly what she intended because it was the same thing that she had done to so many other children.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby P]’s final collapse came at about 3.15 that afternoon and all efforts to resuscitate him failed and [Baby P] was pronounced dead at 4 pm.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: His body was examined by a pathologist, and Dr Kokai concluded that [Baby P] had died from what's called sudden unexpected postnatal collapse. Dr Kokai was unable to identify the underlying cause, and so he certified the cause of death as prematurity.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The medical independent experts have reviewed [Baby P]’s case. Dr Evans initially suggested that the cause of death was complications from the punctured lung, but he was suspicious of the large volume of air in [Baby P]’s stomach and intestines that I've told you about that had been noted from the X-ray. And in his subsequent reports, Dr Evans concluded that excess air in the stomach could have splinted [Baby P]’s diaphragm, which would have compromised his breathing. Do you remember I explained that to you a couple of times before?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin also concluded that the swelling in the abdomen had splinted [Baby P]’s diaphragm and that that had meant that [Baby P] was unable fully to expand his lungs and had led to his collapse. She concluded that subsequent resuscitation and intubation involving high pressures from the ventilator, together with vigorous resuscitation, can cause a punctured lung. So it's the treatment for the problem that was caused by Lucy Letby that had caused the punctured lung, putting it in simple terms.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin described the abnormal gas pattern seen in [Baby P]’s stomach, which ran all the way down his bowel to his rectum, and she concluded that it was caused by somebody injecting him with air through the nasogastric tube. She described that as "the only plausible explanation". That excess air had splinted the diaphragm, compromised [Baby P]’s breathing and had caused his collapse.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The pathologist, Dr Marnerides, thought that on balance the most likely explanation for [Baby P]’s collapse was his having received excessive air injected into his stomach, so he agreed. He concluded that the pneumothorax, the punctured lung, was the consequence of the treatment and he could find no evidence when reviewing the post-mortem examination, no evidence of any clinical disease or trauma, although he did notice an injury to [Baby P]’s liver, but in [Baby P]’s case, as opposed to [Baby O]’s case, where he thought it was trauma, such was the nature
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: of the injuries to [Baby P]’s liver that he thought it was probably the result of CPR rather than a deliberate assault.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Ladies and gentlemen, as with all these cases, it is the coincidence of problems happening when Lucy Letby was about and the coincidence of the same problems happening with different babies at different times which we suggest is so telling and indicates that it was her malign hand at work.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In her interviews insofar as the events of 23 June were concerned, in other words the time that's covered by that feeding chart I showed you at the beginning, Lucy Letby explained that the student nurse fed [Baby P] at two-hourly intervals up to 4 o'clock and that she alone had fed [Baby P] at 6 o'clock, and that corresponds to the initials, doesn't it, at the bottom of the chart?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: With regard to 24 June, the day [Baby P] died, she agreed that she had agreed to be [Baby P]’s designated nurse because the parents had asked for some continuity.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that early in the shift, at about 8 o'clock, she could see loops in his tummy and had brought those to the attention of the doctor. Having seen loops at 8 o'clock in the morning, of course, is what she recorded retrospectively when she made the notes at 9 pm, after the end of the shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: If it was true, and this is another case where we invite you to view her notes with a degree of cynicism, if what she noted was true it would suggest, wouldn't it, that when she took over the care of [Baby P] from the night shift, [Baby P] had a developing problem? But we know that wasn't the case because Sophie Ellis' notes, made at 6.40, say that the issue had been resolved.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As a matter of fact at 8 o'clock when she said she saw the loops of bowel, she was busy sending messages on her phone. The first time [Baby P] was seen by a doctor on that shift was at 9.35 when he was seen by Dr Ukoh. So, ladies and gentlemen, we say this is a clear example of Lucy Letby making factually false entries in the medical records, in effect to cover herself, to make it look like this is all a problem that occurred on somebody else's watch, somebody else's shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby explained that she'd been present to assist the doctors throughout the day as [Baby P] had continued to deteriorate. After he died, she spent time with his parents and at one point took a photograph of both [Baby O] and [Baby P] together in a cot. She denied deliberately causing [Baby P] any harm.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So ladies and gentlemen, to the final count in the indictment, please, count 22, the attempted murder of [Baby Q]. [Baby Q] was born on 22 June, so a day after the [Babies O, P & R] triplets, and Lucy Letby attempted to murder him, we say, on 25 June, which was the day after she had murdered [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby Q]'s parents were [Parents of Baby Q].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby Q] was 31 weeks plus 3 days gestation at birth.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was born in the early hours of the day and he was a reasonably good weight of 2.076 kilos.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He got some breathing support through CPAP for the first 20 hours of life and he was admitted to the neonatal unit because he needed some breathing support.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Initially, he was stable, he had a catheter, a tube, in place through his umbilicus for nutrition, but as it happened he was well enough to start feeding through the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Initially, he was put into room 1 with [Baby R] at a time when [Baby P] and [Baby O] were in room number 2.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When the nursing staff checked [Baby Q]'s NGT on 23 and 24 June, they noticed small amounts of bile, but the amounts weren't sufficiently great to cause concern or to stop him being fed milk and he was still in room 1 at that stage.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On the night shift of the 24th into 25 June, so the shift immediately after [Baby P] had died, [Baby Q]'s designated nurse was Samantha O'Brien, and she monitored [Baby P] through the night and he was being fed the tiny amount of milk of 0.5, one half of 1 millilitre of milk, every 2 hours, at 3 am, 5 am and 7 am on the 25th.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurse O'Brien was content with [Baby Q]'s condition, although his blood gas readings deteriorated slightly, so she referred [Baby Q]'s case to the registrar, [Dr D], and when [Dr D] reviewed [Baby Q] she wasn't at all concerned about him.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So 25 June was a Saturday and that morning, that day shift, Lucy Letby was working and she was [Baby Q]'s designated nurse from 7.30 in the morning. Other nurses working the shift were Minna Lappalainen, who was the shift leader, Mary Griffith, [Nurse B], and Nicola Dennison was the nursery nurse. By the time this shift started, [Baby Q] had been moved from room 1 down to room 2.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 8 o'clock, Lucy Letby made notes on [Baby Q]'s fluid/feeding chart and because he was only taking a tiny amount of milk, he
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: was also being fed Babiven, the total parenteral nutrition. Do you remember that yellow-coloured liquid in a bag that you saw in the video of a couple of days ago, what I was suggesting had had insulin put into it in the case of [Baby F]?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At just after 9 o'clock that morning, that Saturday morning, Lucy Letby and Mary Griffith were together in nursery 2. According to Mary Griffith, Lucy Letby was attending to [Baby Q] and Nurse Griffith herself was attending to the other child in the room.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nine o'clock was, for these children, or for [Baby Q] at least, his feeding time and the time for his observations to be taken. According to the record, the handwritten record, [Baby Q]'s heart and breathing rates both increased over a short period of time after 9 o'clock, which is the feeding time.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But what is actually in the feeding chart is, we suggest, most unusual. I'm going to show you another feeding chart. This is 24331, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'll just run through the same routine, ladies and gentlemen, not because I don't think you understand, it's just to try and reinforce how these things work so that you can hit the ground running when you start to hear the evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Top left-hand corner, name of the child, [Baby Q]. "Day 4" you can see highlighted there. The date on the left-hand side below the name, which is highlighted, 25 June. You can see that the feeding times are inserted along the top row there, every hour, and you can see that the fluid is Babiven via a UVC, which is a line going in through the umbilicus.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You can see there that at 3 o'clock, [Baby Q] was fed half of 1 millilitre of milk. He was fed the same at 5 o'clock and at 7 o'clock, and underneath you see the running total, rising in increments of half a millilitre. You can see the aspirates recorded and highlighted.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But you'll remember what I said about [Baby Q] starting to deteriorate just after the 9 o'clock feed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And if you look right in the bottom line of the chart, you see the signatures or the initials of the nurses.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What you can see is that Lucy Letby, LL, her initials appear first at 8 o'clock, and they're partially obscured by a hole that's been punched in the paper and then photocopied, which is why you have the black circle.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Let's just look at the column for 9 o'clock. You already know enough about how these charts work. If you read down from the top from 9 o'clock, so we're going vertically now, you can see the amount of the Babiven fluid that was being administered, the rate at which it was being administered, but then in the feeding chart -- so that's a note apparently made at 9 o'clock -- [Baby Q] was due to be fed at 9 o'clock. But what do we have?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Absolutely nothing. No note in the milk row at all and it was not initialled either, almost as if something caused her to leave at 9 o'clock before she'd finished making the records.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurse Griffith, who was the other nurse in the room, who had her back to what was going on with [Baby Q] behind her, was asked by Lucy Letby to monitor [Baby Q] while she went to nursery 1 to do cares for another baby. Cares is a term of art which has -- it involves nurses doing a set regime of things for another baby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And she had another baby for whom she was the designated nurse in room number 1.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There's an entry on the other baby's chart at 8.30, so half an hour before this, signed by Lucy Letby and another entry on the other baby's chart in room number 1 at 9 o'clock, which isn't signed, like this one that isn't signed for [Baby Q].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But Lucy Letby did sign on yet another baby's chart, so we've got -- [Baby Q] is baby 1, the baby in room number 1 is the second, and there was a third baby in room 1, the second one in room 1, but the third baby overall, including [Baby Q], which -and Lucy Letby did sign his chart at 9.04.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Anyway, just back to 9 o'clock, so having given you the context of the documents, going back to 9 o'clock when what we see highlighted there is supposed to be going on. Mary Griffith agreed to keep an eye on [Baby Q] figuratively rather than literally, I suppose, because she had her back to him, and continued to do what she was doing with the other child in the room.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: A few minutes later, [Baby Q]'s monitors started to alarm or his monitor started to alarm. We say that what Lucy Letby did to [Baby Q] at 9 o'clock was to inject him down the NGT with air and a clear fluid, whether it was water, whether it was saline, we can't say, but it was a clear fluid. She was trying to kill him.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurse Griffith heard the alarm, she called for help, and she was joined by Nurse Lappalainen, and [Baby Q] had been sick. The nurses used a suction catheter whilst [Baby Q] was given help with his breathing and then Lucy Letby appeared with the
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: doctors, who were responding to the call for help. The doctor's notes indicate that they were called to the unit at 9.17 as [Baby Q] had "just vomited", and his oxygen saturations had dropped to the low 60s, so very low. The medical staff gave [Baby Q] help with his breathing, using the Neopuff device, they cleared his airways with a suction device, and the records show that not only had [Baby Q]'s oxygen rates dropped but his heart rate had dropped as well and he's described as "mottled" in appearance.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When the nasogastric tube was aspirated, the doctors retrieved a substantial amount of air, air that had just been put in there by somebody, we say, because if the feeding regime had been correctly followed at 9 am when Lucy Letby has made a partial note saying she was there, the person who fed or was to feed [Baby Q], ie Lucy Letby, would have aspirated the tube to see if there was anything in his stomach before he should have been fed that minuscule amount, half of 1 millilitre of milk.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There's another chart that was filled in at the time, or another form that was filled in at the time, and I'm going to show you that. It's 24314, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do you remember me telling you that when the alarm went off and Nurse Griffith called for help, Lucy Letby didn't appear, Nurse Lappalainen appeared? This is a chart that's been filled in by Nurse Lappalainen. You can see on the right-hand side in the signature column, her signature. What we see on the left-hand side is the time and date: 25 June, 9.10. This is a form which is designed to record if a child stops breathing, has a low heart rate or has a fit.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We can see the heart rate -- this is a low heart rate for such a small child -- of 98. You can see the desaturation down to 68%, "Query fit?", then, "Duration: 3 minutes intermittently".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then what we have noted by Nurse Lappalainen is:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Baby found to be very mucousy, clear mucus from nasopharynx/oropharynx removed. Clear fluid+++."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lots of clear fluid coming out of the airway of this small baby:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "O2 [oxygen] via Neopuff."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So oxygen given using the Neopuff device -- sorry, given postsuctioning:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "[Dr A], emergency call to attend."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "NGT [nasogastric tube] used to aspirate stomach by nurse L Letby."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Given that Lucy Letby was [Baby Q]'s designated nurse on this shift, and that she performed the aspiration of air, you might think it is a little surprising that it wasn't her that actually made the note. And yet she did make notes in the records of other babies at about the same time. And we question whether this is an attempt by her to create a documentary alibi, so if ever anyone went back to the records to see who was dealing with [Baby Q] at the time, who would they think it was? She's alibied herself in the third child's notes by making a note at 09.04. So we suggest a cynical and fairly sophisticated way of making the notes appear as if she had nothing to do with what was going on.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The computerised notes that Lucy Letby made for that morning's events recorded this, and I'll quote -- I won't show you this one, I'll just tell you what it said. It says this:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "At 9.10, [Baby Q] attended to by Nurse Lappalainen. He had vomited clear fluid nasally and from mouth, desaturation and bradycardia [so low heart rate] mottled++. Neopuff and suction applied. Registrar [Dr A] attended. Air++..."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So one fewer plus in her notes than -- it may mean nothing:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "... aspirated from NG tube."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Following [Baby Q]'s collapse, blood was taken to test for infection and a test of that blood suggested that he was unwell. Whatever the problem was, it had resolved by 11.12. [Baby Q] was started on a course of antibiotics as a precaution and [Dr A]'s recorded view at the time was that [Baby Q]'s collapse was a result of presumed sepsis with jaundice.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: A chest X-ray taken at the time showed nothing untoward and more detailed blood tests were recorded at 1.50 in the afternoon that showed slightly abnormal results, which were treated, and [Baby Q] made a reasonable recovery through the day.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: By the end of the shift, at 7.20, he was described as looking tired and doctors took the decision to intubate him because his respiratory rate had dropped to 19, which is low, and his heart rate was high, between 160 and 200 beats per minute. But despite that, his blood gas readings were good.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We say, ladies and gentlemen, that when she went home that night, Lucy Letby was worried. She must have got the impression that people were becoming suspicious of what she had been doing
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: and she texted [Dr A] at 10.09 -- sorry, at 10.46, so quarter to 11 that evening, and asked this question:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Do I need to be worried about what Dr Gibbs was asking?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And [Dr A] sought to put her mind at rest and told her that Dr Gibbs was only asking to make sure that the normal procedures had been carried out. And she replied to [Dr A] that after [Baby Q] had collapsed she, Lucy Letby, had walked into the equipment room and [Dr A] had been asking Mary Griffith, who had been present in the room when [Baby Q] had collapsed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry, do you mean [Dr A]?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I beg your pardon, Dr Gibbs. So she is speaking to [Dr A]. What she asked [Dr A] or what she told [Dr A] was that after [Baby Q] had collapsed, when she'd walked into the equipment room, Dr Gibbs had been asking Mary Griffith, who had been present in the room when [Baby Q] collapsed, how quickly someone had gone to him because she, Lucy Letby, hadn't been there.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She continued her text to [Dr A], telling him that she had needed to go to another designated child in room number 1, which of course was the excuse that she had given to Mary Griffith at the time.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, the next day, so far as [Baby Q] was concerned, at 6.50 that morning, [Baby Q]'s blood gases were unsatisfactory, but it was noted by [Dr D], who was on duty, that [Baby Q] had had the tube removed 4 hours earlier and he was in air, breathing for himself and had good oxygen saturation, so a good sign.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Medical staff on that shift noted a mildly dilated loop of bowel on his left side and raised the possibility that perhaps he had NEC. Do you remember that bowel disorder? So [Baby Q] was transferred to Alder Hey Hospital in Liverpool, the children's hospital in Liverpool, and you know what I'm going to say. He quickly stabilised, no surgery proved necessary, and the breathing support was removed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He returned to the Countess of Chester on 28 June and he, we say, was yet another child who suffered life-threatening problems. Investigations at the time could find no issue and when he was moved out of the orbit of Lucy Letby, he made a rapid recovery.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Other than 3 days the following week, that was the last time that Lucy Letby worked in the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So far as the expert review of [Baby Q]'s case is concerned, in the opinion of Dr Dewi Evans, [Baby Q]'s collapse on the morning of the 25th was due to inappropriate care. He believed that [Baby Q] had been injected with air through his NGT. He thought that the significant amount of air that had been aspirated from his stomach couldn't have arisen in any other way because [Baby Q] hadn't been receiving any breathing assistance and was being fed only minuscule amounts of milk.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The "clear fluid+++" noted by Minna Lappalainen that was vomited by [Baby Q] had to have been given to him by somebody because it wasn't going in as feed. It had to get in there to come out, didn't it, and it hadn't been part of the half of 1 millilitre of milk. And Dr Evans thought that therefore it had to be either normal water or saline, the sort of water that is used in medical treatment, salty water.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The stomach findings, thought Dr Evans, were not explicable by his bowel condition. He didn't have a bowel condition, but were consistent with [Baby Q] having received a lot of air through the NGT and some clear fluid some time before 9.10 that morning.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin noted that [Baby Q] was well up until events on 25 June and she also concluded that something happened at about 9 o'clock. She made the same points as Dr Evans about what he was being fed, what was going in and what came out. She also remarked on the large volume of air that was suctioned from or aspirated from [Baby Q] and concluded that a lot of air in the stomach would have splinted the diaphragm, which would have squashed the lungs, which would have compromised [Baby Q]'s breathing.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In dealing with the fact that [Baby Q] wasn't particularly well for the rest of the day, she concluded that although a baby may recover quickly after such an event, the baby may remain unstable for some time thereafter.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: An expert neuroradiologist, so a doctor with a particular expertise in interpreting scans of the brain, Dr Stavros Stivaros, reviewed brain imaging of [Baby Q] that had been taken in November 2019, so more than 3 years later, and he found evidence of abnormalities in [Baby Q]'s brain which, whilst they were not diagnostic of him having suffered a brain injury as a result of being given excessive air and liquid, were explicable by such an event having occurred. So abnormalities of the brain, you can't say what the definite cause of that is, being given excess air and liquid, but what he could say was that finding is consistent with that having happened.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was questioned about these events. Her home was searched. In the search of her home the police found the
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: handover sheet, the sheet that the nurses get of the patients and the designated nurses from the shift on which we say she sabotaged [Baby Q] on the 25th. And like the others, it's a document which shouldn't have left the hospital. To be fair, she had a lot of these documents at home.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When she was interviewed by police, Lucy Letby agreed that [Baby Q] had been well enough for her to have left him at just after 9 o'clock on the morning of the 25th. When she was asked about the excess air aspirated from his stomach, she suggested that sometimes babies gulp air when they vomit. Well, it was the air and the liquid that caused him to vomit, it wasn't the result of the vomit, we say. She denied putting excess air down his nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's all I have to say about [Baby Q]'s case at this stage, ladies and gentlemen. I'm just going to say a few words in conclusion, pretty quickly.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Following events in that year, between June 2015 and June 2016, the consultants at the Countess of Chester suspected that the deaths and the life-threatening events of these 17 children were not medically explicable but were the result of the actions of Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No doubt they were acutely aware that making that sort of an allegation against a nurse was as serious as it gets. They, at the time, didn't have the benefit of the evidence that you are going to hear and the decision that was taken by the hospital at the time was to remove her from a hands-on role and she was moved to clerical duties where she wouldn't come into contact with children.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The police were contacted and they conducted a lengthy and complex inquiry. That involved the instruction of the doctors that I have referred to already to review many cases which had passed through the neonatal unit in Chester, and following that review, the decision was taken to arrest Lucy Letby and, as I have already told you, I think, the first arrest took place in July 2018.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The first arrest was 3 July 2018. It took place at her home at 41 Westbourne Road in Chester and the house was searched. As I have already told you, a large quantity of paperwork from the hospital was recovered.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In addition to the paperwork relating to some of the children I have told you about and other children, they also found some other interesting items. There were some Post-it notes. You know what I mean, those little yellow tabular notes, with closely written words on them, some of which included the names of her
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: colleagues. On some of the notes were phrases like: Why?" How has this happened? What process has led to this current situation? What allegations have been made and by whom? Do they have written evidence to support their comments?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In her writings, she expressed frustration at the fact that she wasn't being allowed back on to the neonatal unit and she wrote:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "I haven't done anything wrong and they have no evidence, so why have I had to hide away?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And her notes also expressed concern for the long-term effects of what she feared was being alleged against her. There are also many protestations of innocence. But I want to show you one note in particular and it's J321.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think it's 312 just for the record.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There's all sorts of material on this document. But just where that cross is now, just to the right of that, it says:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "I don't deserve to live. I killed them on purpose because I'm not good enough to care for them. I am a horrible, evil person."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At the bottom:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "I am evil. I did this."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, ladies and gentlemen, that, in a nutshell, is your task in this case. You have to decide on the evidence whether she did do these things or any of them.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's important to remember that the prosecution brings this case and therefore we, the prosecution, must prove it. And in order to prove it, we must make you sure.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, thank you, Mr Johnson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: What will happen shortly is that Mr Myers will address you, not at the length that you've been addressed by Mr Johnson, but just essentially to explain to you, as I understand it, the defence in this case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That will take -- I think Mr Myers you indicated about an hour and a half, something like that?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Up to 2 hours, my Lord. It may be that I can deal with half of it before lunch and finish the other half afterwards.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I thought that's exactly what we'll do.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We'll have a comfort break now for 10 minutes or so and then at the end of that, when Mr Myers has completed his address this afternoon, we will then take stock of the situation at that point, all right, in relation to you remaining a jury of 14? Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So just 10 or so minutes now, as long as is needed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
Thank you.
I wonder whether we could have a slightly longer break. I've been asked to go down and see Ms Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I picked that up because I can see and hear things that are going on. Certainly, you should be afforded that facility. I'm just thinking of the jury, the mechanics of you getting down there, speaking, coming back up again is going to take quite a long time, I think.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Probably about 30 minutes, my Lord, to deal with it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Don't worry.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Could you please, usher, very kindly -- is there a better room the jury can go to? Just say I've been informed the break will be longer, it's going to be a longer break than 10 minutes, it'll be at least half an hour, and I'll keep them informed in about half an hour if we're not ready. All right. Thank you. And you'll keep the court informed, I know.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Of course, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Ms Letby, your lawyers are going to come down and see you and speak to you, all right, if that's what you want. Just check that is what she wants.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's what we'll do. Can we keep the arrangement as it is, my Lord, and we'll deal with it?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you very much. You can always communicate with me.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (A short break)
My Lord, we're grateful for the opportunity to speak with Ms Letby. In fact, it was something which did not take long and it was an organisational matter.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We dealt with it upstairs, in fact. She spoke to us from the dock and we understand it has been resolved.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But we are grateful for that. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's all right, thank you. Well, when the jury comes back in, Mr Myers, you just choose an appropriate moment around 1 o'clock. If it's slightly after 1 o'clock, don't worry about that. Just whatever's the most convenient time to break off.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
Yes, Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Opening by MR MYERS
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: May it please you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's difficult, ladies and gentlemen, to think of allegations that could be more upsetting than these allegations and it's difficult to think of allegations that strike harder at our desire to protect than these allegations and it's difficult to think of allegations that make it harder to stand back and look fairly at the actual evidence than these allegations.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The sympathy of everyone will rightly be with the families whose children are involved in this case and for those children. We all share the same feelings and the same experiences. We all have families, parents, children of our own or children that we know. It's natural to sympathise, we'll all do it, we're all made of the same stuff. So we recognise the sadness and the distress, and even the anger, that comes with allegations like these and I start, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the defence by acknowledging how upsetting the allegations will be and by acknowledging the very great loss and sadness to the families involved. And nothing that we do, the defence, or I do or say in this trial is intended to diminish that in any way.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's obvious to us, as it will be obvious to anyone listening to this case, and it will be obvious to every one of you, ladies and gentlemen, that where we have such terrible allegations, it would be terribly easy to let emotion take the place of reason and to want to convict without even hearing a word of evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It would be easy and staggeringly unfair.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Each of you has come forward to sit as a juror in this trial and you will know, ladies and gentlemen, that we haven't come to a trial for up to 6 months because we are here to rubber-stamp an allegation and you're not going to give up months of your time to do that. And that has to be said at the outset in a case like this where there has been a lengthy investigation and a huge prosecution mounted and the allegations are so upsetting.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We identify this right at the start: there is a real danger that people will simply accept the prosecution theory of guilt. That's all that we have so far, ladies and gentlemen: a theory of guilt based firmly on coincidence, if anything can be based firmly on coincidence, and we are grateful to his Lordship for the direction given to you at the start of the trial to consider and judge the evidence calmly, rationally, fairly and dispassionately. My goodness, it needs that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: When we do that, or when you do, and if you find that things have gone wrong in these cases or any of them that we're looking at, it is important to be careful that blame is not heaped on that woman (indicating) when there may be others who have made mistakes or a system that has failed or where, actually, in truth, we cannot be sure what happened but what we're left with is coincidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: What the defence say, ladies and gentlemen, is that in the events we'll be looking at in this trial, sometimes what happened was the result of a genuine deterioration in the health of one or other of these children. And sometimes, in fact, nobody can really say why a particular baby deteriorated or died as she or he did, although the pressure to find a fault-based explanation is powerful.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But also, we say that sometimes things have gone wrong or the necessary standards of care have not been met, irrespective of anything to do with Ms Letby, and when that has happened or may have happened, she should not get the blame if she is not responsible.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And it is amazing, isn't it, how with allegations like these, everyone turns and focuses on Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Some people, we say, at the outset, with the rather trusting presumption that because the allegation is brought that she is guilty, she must be guilty, and the worse it sounds, the more guilty she must be.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We and you will be focusing on Ms Letby too, but we will also keep our attention on the surrounding picture, insofar as we can see it, and it's relevant, and you may wish to do that too.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You know, ladies and gentlemen, I defend Ms Letby together with Mr Maher and Ms Clancy, and we are grateful to the court for this opportunity to introduce the defence case to you. At this early stage of the trial I'm going to identify key issues, so far as the defence are concerned, and to outline the response to the prosecution case. But as you know, it is only an outline.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The purpose of that is to assist you in following the evidence when we come to it so that you can weigh it up and you have an idea of the things that the defence are focusing upon and you can put everything into context.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Over the past 3 days, or 4 days in fact, you've heard the prosecution opening speech setting out their case in detail, and of course it's lengthy because they have a lot of detail they want to show to you. We're not complaining about that, but what I'm about to say to you is not a defence speech in that way, where I explain to you in detail why we say Lucy Letby is not guilty.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That comes much later in the trial, so please don't think that at this point I am saying all that there is to be said. I am barely touching on it. There's massive detail in this case. Without the detail, the allegations do not count.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: This is not a defence equivalent of what you've been listening to from the prosecution, but the rules allow for the defence to introduce the issues in the case from the defence point of view at this point, so that's what I'm going to do and it will take no more than a couple of hours. It will go up to lunchtime, then a break, and then I can carry on afterwards and finish in the first part of this afternoon, give or take a bit. You'll find the timings, although we do our best, can sometimes be a bit imprecise, but that's roughly how long.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So I emphasise again, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the defence, I will be talking to you about why Lucy Letby is not guilty a good deal longer when we get to the end of the case. This is just a brief introduction.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There will be a lot to look at in this trial, but having set this out in outline now, you will have a better idea of what to
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: expect and what to look out for and the general nature of the defence response. What I'm going to do this morning and into this afternoon is just break down what I'm going to say into three general areas.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The first one, Lucy Letby and the general nature of her defence and some issues relating to her. Then we'll have a look at what the defence say about coincidence, and then we'll have a look at the medical evidence, only a brief one, it's enormous, but just a quick look so you can understand where the defence are coming from with this.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We suggest, ladies and gentlemen, that the medical evidence is a key area in this case and so when I come to that, which might be this afternoon, or it will be, I'll try to assist you by setting out the overall areas to focus on and then go to key issues on each count.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And it is really just an outline so you have an understanding of the type of issues and the way this will go when we get to the evidence. Don't worry about, for example, trying to absorb the detail of everything from this. It's entirely up to you what you note or what you do with what I say, but it's really just to help you so you can see, all right, the prosecution have said that, this is the sort of thing the defence or their experts are going to say when they're dealing with the issues on that count.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So I'll be going through them almost like bullet points, but since one of the purposes of this is to simplify it by identifying issues to help you and the court with what we are looking for, that's what I'll do when I come to that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We'll also touch on issues in relation to Ms Letby's presence or absence at the time of events in the indictment and finally introduce you to what we say is a potentially relevant question with respect to failings in care at the Countess of Chester Hospital Neonatal Unit that have nothing to do with Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So let me start with the general nature of the defence case and Ms Letby. What is the defence case?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, the defence say that Lucy Letby was a dedicated nurse. She trained hard to become a neonatal nurse and what she wanted was to care for the babies she looked after and we say she did her best to do so for years and in no way did she want to harm them.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The defence say Lucy Letby is not guilty of intentionally causing any harm to any baby or intentionally killing any baby and, so far as she knows, she hasn't caused harm.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Her case is that she was a dedicated nurse who loved her job, who cared deeply about the babies she looked for, and cared also about their families. She lived a fulfilling life with friends, a life outside of her work, but a life where her work was what she was dedicated to. You might well have taken a good look at Lucy Letby in the time we've already had in this trial, but you know, ladies and gentlemen, you won't get the answer to this case or the answers simply by looking at that woman in the dock now.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: This is how she is now and where she is, you will keep in mind, 6 years after starting to face allegations like this, and you can imagine that must be utterly gruelling for anyone.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You may want to keep the effect of that in mind as we go through the evidence in this case and when you come to assess things she has said or says and how she is now. And this is an important part of her case, so I identify it now: the requirement to keep context in mind and to distinguish how she was at the time events took place compared with how she is now.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You will want to keep in mind what this must be like: a young woman had trained hard to be a nurse, who had worked for qualifications for years, and who cared for very many vulnerable babies for years.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say a woman who loved what she did, who then discovered she was being blamed for the deaths of babies she cared for. It's important to keep this in mind at the beginning, with these allegations: we are dealing with a real person who is where she is now, the defence say, because of a litany of allegations that are extraordinary, far from straightforward and, crucially, not one of which has yet been proved. Anybody who approaches this as if it's some sort of done deal has got this very badly wrong.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So we ask you to keep that in mind and the effect of the allegations which, you may agree, will be very powerful and keep that in mind when looking at various parts of the case relating to various things she has said or done after she began to face the allegations.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And by way of example, let me take you back to that note we looked at just before the break, J312, please.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If we can just enlarge it. I'll come to what we say about the content in a moment. Just enlarge it first, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The prosecution finished their opening speech with this, so let me by way of introduction deal with what we say about it, although you will look at this with your own views and experiences of life and other notes like it because you'll not -
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: - not the same context but other notes from Ms Letby during the case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It was introduced as evidence supportive of guilt, the prosecution would say. We suggest that anyone who reads this fully, with an ounce of human understanding, will appreciate that this is the anguished outpouring of a young woman in fear and despair when she realises the enormity of what is being said about her and this is her way of expressing it, in the moment, to herself.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Before I come to some of what's there, it's important, ladies and gentlemen, that you know that before her first arrest in July 2018, there was a period during 2016 and onwards when Lucy Letby was dealing with issues in relation to her employment. So this is after she'd come off clinical duties but before the police were ever involved, dealing with issues in relation to her employment and going through a grievance procedure with the NHS trust, and that that was when she discovered what was being said about her. This will emerge so it's important to put these things into context so you can fit them together, ladies and gentlemen.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So she knew what was being said before arrest and we say the impact of that and those allegations was devastating and destructive, and with that in mind we then ask you briefly just to look at the note we have here. You will see at the top it doesn't say guilty, it says "Not good enough".
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: To the right-hand side:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "An awful person. I pay every day for that right now. I'll never have children or marry, I'll never know what it's like to have a family. Despair."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Opposite that on the left-hand side:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "I haven't done anything wrong."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Go through and pick out one bit, pick out another bit, pick out what you like. You know, ladies and gentlemen, that when someone's upset very badly, they can scribble thoughts and feelings that reflect how they feel, even though what they write may not accurately reflect what is going on around them or has gone on.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You will have to assess this type of thing when presented with this type of material in this case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say people can pour their feelings on to paper as a way of coping and it's the outpouring that matters.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And we say this note reflects the anguished state of mind that Ms Letby found herself in, how she felt when she learnt she was being accused of killing children she believed she'd done her best to care for.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I will have a lot more to say about this on behalf of the defence and Ms Letby when we get to the end of this trial, but for now, we say that what you see there is anguish, not guilt. We can take that down, I'm going to move on, please. Thank you, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Can I ask, before deciding what you make of the notes and other notes taken from Ms Letby, that you wait until we get to the end of the evidence? That's so important. By that stage of the case, you will probably know a lot more about her and what she'd been through and the case in general and what you make of it than you can possibly know at the moment, what anyone listening to this can possibly know at the moment. That is a more balanced and appropriate way of putting this note and the evidence in this case in context generally.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There will be other notes and papers to look at during this trial. There was a substantial amount of paperwork taken from Ms Letby's home once the police became involved in the investigation and arrested her and took her away to be interviewed. When it comes to all these notes and papers, you may well want to ask whether Ms Letby had them in her possession for a sinister motive, which is the thrust of what the prosecution say on many aspects of them, or whether she had them simply because she is one of those people both who scribbles things down a lot on paper, we say you will see that, and who hangs on to pieces of paper that come into her possession afterwards. And it's nothing more extraordinary than that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'm aware this is only an introduction to the case and you'll understand that I'm not by any measure going into everything we would like to say or plan to say at the conclusion when you have the benefit of the evidence. I'm going to move to the next topic I identified, which is coincidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The prosecution has spoken at length about coincidence and so we turn to that next and we identify how the defence respond to that so that you can keep this in mind and measure this against what you see in the course of the trial.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say, ladies and gentlemen, that this prosecution case is driven by the assumption that someone was doing deliberate harm, that assumption of deliberate harm combined with the coincidence on certain occasions of Ms Letby's presence. Two things. I'll repeat that and then we can come back to it at various points.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But we say there is an assumption that someone is doing deliberate harm. Start with that or have that in mind and then have a look and find the coincidence apparently of Ms Letby and the two things are then put together.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's important in identifying this and I will explain further what we mean.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Can I start with this. What it isn't driven by, ladies and gentlemen, is evidence of Ms Letby actually doing what is alleged against her. So I ask you to absorb that. When we turn to the evidence time and time again there is in fact, when you look back at what you've heard already, it would appear, no evidence of the actual acts being alleged.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: For all the assumptions and coincidences, you will find, from what we have heard, no evidence of her actually doing harm to any child. I'll expand upon what I mean by that. These allegations are allegations of attacks. You've heard the prosecution use words like poisoning, attacking, even sabotage, repeatedly.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Powerful words that are likely to have had a powerful emotional impact on you and anyone who hears them.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But you will want to weigh that against whether or not in the course of this case reference can be made to any piece of evidence that actually shows Ms Letby engaged in any of the attacks alleged. So we identify this now so you can keep this firmly in mind when we proceed through the case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Using syringes to inject air. No, we say.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Tampering with bags of fluid. No. Or in some other way poisoning them. No. Physically assaulting children, smothering them.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We are dealing with 24 events and the defence will say the prosecution do not describe in opening anything that is in that territory. And we identify that now, we say it is significant. And by way of an illustration of the type of process we say you will need to apply to this, do you remember what the prosecution said in reference to [Mother of Babies E & F], the mother of [Baby E] and [Baby F], who they say was there as Lucy Letby was attacking [Baby E]? Do you remember that, that Lucy Letby was in the course of attacking [Baby E] when his mother came in and she was just fobbed off?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We'll come to that in due course and when we do, you may want to ask, by way of an example, whether that evidence actually shows Lucy Letby attacking a baby in front of his mother or not. When
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: you hear the allegations, we ask you to measure them against the evidence you will hear.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So considering assumption and coincidence, can I enlarge upon what we mean when we describe an assumption of guilt? We say that in this case, there is a danger that the theory that intentional harm was done, combined with the assumption that if Lucy Letby is there, she must be doing that harm, has made the allegations self-fulfilling. In other words, and you measure the evidence against this, the fact that Lucy Letby has been present at the time there has been a deterioration in the health of a child has itself become an explanation for that deterioration even though we say, we ask you to look for this, there is no evidence to show that she has caused that to happen.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Which brings us back to coincidence and I would like us to look, if we could, at the chart the prosecution rely on in this area, CEH16A. You will remember this, ladies and gentlemen, you'll probably see it during the course of this case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Because of that, and because we have the opportunity now to outline the defence response and the issues that arise, I would like to tell what you we say about this because this is, it would seem, central to what the prosecution say.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say that when we look at this it is important to keep in mind, first of all, that this table exists because the prosecution created it and it has been put together by the prosecution for the purpose of this prosecution.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It contains material selected with a view to showing that Lucy Letby was present at time of what had been declared to be the key events or suspicious events. Of course, ladies and gentlemen, the prosecution are entitled to do this, it is their case they bring and this is a way they have chosen to represent what they say is the evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In response to that, the defence will say that to a large extent this is a self-serving document and the defence will say what we have here is presented like this because the prosecution have chosen to present it this way.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: What it shows are what the prosecution say are events when intentional harm was done to the babies named and what they say is the coincidence with the presence on the unit. Now, in identifying where the issues lie and the defence response to this fairly central piece of evidence, we identify the following: what this table doesn't show, and the sort of things you may want to look for in evidence when we actually come to it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It doesn't show the actual health or condition of the child concerned. It doesn't show any problems that child had from birth and what risks followed on from those. It doesn't show the course of treatment and problems encountered during that period. Some of the periods are quite lengthy and you will find very much more went on than the incidents or the aspects of them that you have focused on so far.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We recognise, in fairness, the prosecution have to deliver an
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: opening speech in a reasonable period of time. If they went

through everything, it would be like doing the trial twice. But we say it is important when we're identifying the things to look at, you will need to look at the course of treatment and the problems over that period.

It doesn't show whether there had been other desaturations or collapses on other occasions when Lucy Letby wasn't present. It shows the ones where, by the plotting, something happens which the prosecution say is significant and she is there. It doesn't show if there may be other significant events, the defence say, and this will be for the evidence, when she wasn't there.

We do say there have been other events in the course of many of these babies' histories. You don't know about them yet, but we'll come to it in the evidence, which is one of the reasons why it will take time and it will have to be detailed. Now you know one of the ways in which we say that will be relevant and you know what to look for.

It doesn't include shortcomings in care that may be the fault of others and which may have had an impact on that particular baby. It doesn't show the impact of how busy the unit was at the time the events happened, it doesn't show how busy the unit was, and it certainly doesn't show what Lucy Letby was actually doing at the time of a particular event. These are all the sort of things you may think it's going to be important to look out for in the evidence, wherever that takes you, because they are, you may think, important things. It may make you more or less confident of what the prosecution say, but they are important parts of the case.

It doesn't show whether or not Ms Letby was anywhere near to a child at the time of an event and it doesn't show how, as the defence will say, there are some occasions when a problem can be traced, the start of a problem can be traced to a point before Ms Letby was ever actually either on duty or near to that child.
There is a massive amount it doesn't contain.
When we come to look at the defence case, what the defence cannot do on every occasion is to explain why certain children

deteriorated or died and actually nobody here would say that Ms Letby has to be able to do so. This is something that's been quite a difficult question even for the experts in this case. As someone who's done their best to look after children in their care, the defence would say they may very well not have an explanation for what had happened.
I have spent a little time outlining some aspects of the defendant's case and what we say about this table.

We can take that down for now, please, Mr Murphy. What about other areas the defence say are key areas to focus on? In particular I'm referring to the medical evidence and evidence relating to Lucy Letby's presence at the time of various events. Can I say, by the way, ladies and gentlemen, there are obviously far more areas and aspects to this case than just those two or the ones we've been looking at. But we are going to suggest that when we strip away all the surrounding detail -- messages, Facebook searches, pieces of paper, even amateur psychology -what the case will come down to is the medical evidence. That's what we say. That's the key material in this case, the medical evidence and what it can safely prove and what it can't, and the question of what we can safely conclude from the evidence of Ms Letby's presence or not.

We don't say the other areas of evidence are unimportant, they may be, you will make of them what you wish. They may be important for both sides in this case, but what we do say is that the foundation of the case is the expert medical evidence and the question of coincidence.

So medical evidence and the general approach to that. We say that in the case of these children, ladies and gentlemen, the cause of deterioration or death is not always clear from the medical evidence and there may be on occasions be a number of possibilities. You will need to keep this in mind, it might have struck you already: generally, we are dealing with babies who are clinically fragile and their condition can change very swiftly and when that happens they are capable of deteriorating very rapidly.

You've heard about babies who are premature or may be called preterm. Some are very preterm, extremely preterm, low birth weight. Both conditions like that can be accompanied by serious developmental or health problems: struggling to breathe, not able to breathe unaided, desaturating, dropping in oxygen, time and again, whether or not Ms Letby is there. You have heard about babies like that, you've heard about babies who one, [Baby H], required chest drains. A baby who had undergone surgery, leaving her with two stomas, which means, as you now know, if you didn't before, the passage of material that would pass
through the bowel outside the body. Babies fed by tube. Receiving nutrition intravenously. Infections.

It is crucial to keep in mind the starting point in these cases. We also say there is a question as to whether this hospital should have been looking after all of these children and whether it did so to the required standards. That is something you might want to look at.
There is so much more to the evidence in this case than simply coincidence, something happened, guilt.

When we're dealing with children like this, ladies and gentlemen, there will be deteriorations. There will. And the cause may not always be clear. Just because the cause may not be clear, that is no basis for guilt and, as we may see in this case, in medicine the explanation for why things happen is not always clear and there is not always one possible explanation. But where that uncertainty is combined with a suspicion or an assumption that what has happened may be the result of an assault, then that assumption may become the explanation even though nobody can say for sure what has happened.

We suggest, ladies and gentlemen, that there are times in this case, and again we identify this now and we will ask you to keep this in mind when we get to the evidence, when an event that clearly fits an ongoing and clinically difficult condition of a particular baby has been converted into an event of deep suspicion because of the assumption that harm is being done.

In a way, by way of illustration, you saw that at work repeatedly at certain points in the prosecution opening with all those lead-ups -- you remember the lines about "And you know what happened next"? What did happen next? What happened next, in fact, when that was said, was Lucy Letby standing there doing none of the specific acts alleged against her, however unexpectedly someone came into the room. Not one.

For a nurse in a neonatal unit standing there when a child is unwell is unremarkable, unless you are going to approach this with an assumption of guilt combined with a mere fact that her presence alone is now treated as sinister, whether or not the evidence shows her doing anything.
So we need to look at the medical evidence very closely and the expert medical evidence in particular.

When we come to that, ladies and gentlemen, the experts, you will need to look at their opinions and how strong the basis for them is. That's what the evidence is for and we'll spend a lot of time looking at it. And for those people who are not doctors
or nurses, which must be most of us in this courtroom, but maybe not all of us, it may look daunting to start with, but as we go along you will become increasingly comfortable with looking at it.

The defence ask you to consider five issues when we come to the medical evidence -- I'm going to home in now and identify issues with the medical evidence in particular -- five issues that we say are important in each case. Again, there may be some overlap. I'm going to list them, say a little about each one, and in particular some detail about the medical explanations for the events when we get to it. A lot to take in, compressed into a period of time, but if, when we finish, you have at least a better idea of what the type of issues are, what the responses will be and the type of things to look for, that will help, and then, as we go along during the case, we'll keep returning to the sort of issues we're looking at with different children, often with the same expert witnesses, and you will become increasingly familiar with what both prosecution and defence are saying.
The five areas we identify as important and important issues are, first of all, the birth condition of the baby we are looking at. That must surely be relevant.

Secondly, whether there were any problems in the health or care of the child we're looking at, leading up to the event we are considering. Time and again the prosecution identify these events by saying, "What happened was quite unexpected, it came out of nowhere".
