Well, in fact, we say, first of all, things with babies like this can be unexpected and they can come out of nowhere. But we also say, when you get down to the detail of the evidence, it's not always that clear and it isn't always unexpected if you look closely, if you actually look at the information that's available.
That's the second point.

Third, whether the prosecution expert medical evidence proves there was deliberate harm done. Pretty central, that one. And when I come to that, which will be after lunchtime, ladies and gentlemen, as I've said, I'll indicate the defence response to what the prosecution experts say where we can do that. But I will be doing so in bullet form, I won't be going through, spending the time the prosecution did. Again, I know you know, but that's because this is meant to be an outline, it's not a speech with all the detail in.
That comes at the end. That's something to look forward to or to face with trepidation, we'll see, but that comes at the end of this. That's when you'll be in a position to weigh it up.
The fourth matter is this: whether Lucy Letby was present at the relevant time and what the evidence can establish about what she was doing if she was there.

And finally, we suggest you're going to want to consider whether there were failings in care by other people involved with the baby we're looking at or by the unit as a whole. I'll return to that towards the end of what I'm going to say this afternoon. It was just touched on once or twice by the prosecution in their opening. It's going to be more than touched on by us.
I will just deal with the first one of those if I may, my Lord.
Certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That is the birth condition of the babies themselves. I have touched on this previously, so I can deal with it relatively briefly, but it is important.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's really important because it establishes a starting point in terms of what might be expected in the course of that child's care.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Remember, ladies and gentlemen, in this case we are dealing with some of the most medically fragile babies, some of them, that can survive post birth as a result of intensive medical care. Not all of them come into that category but a number of them do. Some aren't on such a cliff edge but all of them bar one are premature to varying degrees and some had potentially significant problems in addition to the mere fact of prematurity and low birth weight.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The defence ask you to look for evidence relating to that and we say it is important because in many cases these babies are already at risk of deterioration and when it happens it can be unexpected and it can be rapid. Over and again you hear allegations based upon how unexpected an event was and how quick it was. We submit that, and we'll suggest to you, that very often that can happen with children like this. We are not starting from a baseline of what could be considered good health in any ordinary sense of that word and you will, of course, listen with interest to those medical experts who tell you how well these children were doing.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: My Lord, I wonder if I could pause.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly, if that's convenient for you, Mr Myers. It's very close to 1 o'clock.

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

I didn't mention, Mr Johnson, this morning, about the glossary. You'll remember there was going to have to be one amendment to that, but it's not important.

blocks.text: Ladies and gentlemen, I'd said there were five issues or areas just to keep in mind when we get to the real substance of the case so far as medical evidence is concerned. I said they were the birth condition of the baby, problems in the health or care of the child we are looking at leading up to the event, medical evidence about the event, and then questions relating to the presence of Lucy Letby at the relevant time and then, finally, any relevant failings in care by people around her or the unit.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We got to the second of those, which is the question of matters leading up to the event we're looking at.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: When we refer to that, ladies and gentlemen, we are looking at the medical situation which leads up to that event and, again, it's a little bit like the first one where I was asking you to keep in mind the condition of a particular child from birth. When we look at the history of them, you may hear witnesses say -- all sorts of witnesses will come and say how well a child was doing and how unexpected the event was and the reasoning being that if a deterioration is unexpected then it must be down to Lucy Letby interfering with that baby with the intention of killing it. Because that's the allegation that's what has to be proved.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, again, being sensible, in most cases we are hardly starting from a baseline of robust good health and we suggest you will need to look very carefully at what has happened on the way to each of the events that we look at, remembering how quickly problems can develop and also, and this may be important, that sometimes the ability to identify problems before they escalate depends on doctors and nurses watching closely, spotting it, recording it, communicating it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: These sort of points that I'm making probably sound a bit general and unrelated from anything, but when we get to the evidence and we return to looking at what happened, hopefully you'll remember that we've identified this kind of thing as something that could be important. And the business of watching closely, recording and identifying may be difficult if a unit is understaffed and overstretched. You may just want to listen out for any evidence that relates to that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So I'm going to come to the third area, which is the area of the expert medical evidence, particularly prosecution expert medical evidence, and whether it can prove that deliberate harm was done. This is a critical area in the case and I'm sure it's one we will look at very closely.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: What the experts do is to work generally by looking at the birth condition of the baby whom they are concerned with, looking at the course of the care and any health problems leading up to the event, looking at all that clinical history, and then in the sad event of a death, the pathology. We'll get the technical descriptions of what these mean, but I'm sure you'll have a good idea of what we mean by pathology, the findings, sadly, after death, when that has happened, and then they tell us what can be established about the cause. It is after they have done that you will hear them say, well, it was this mechanism or that mechanism and it was done deliberately.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, the defence say this is an area too where we have to be careful about the assumption of guilt or the influence of a theory of guilt. In the context of medical evidence, the dangers are opinion being influenced by an overarching assumption that what has happened is because of deliberate harm rather than naturally or a mistake. In other words, happening almost the wrong way round. If someone goes into it with that expectation, is that what they're going to end up seeing?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say that if an expert -- and the fact they're an expert doesn't mean this cannot happen. If an expert sets out with an expectation or a suspicion of harm having been done, or even, in a way, positively going out to look for that, that may make it more likely that he or she will reach explanations that are harm-based whilst rejecting alternatives that may provide an innocent explanation, we are not even thinking about it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And where there is no clear explanation for what has happened, and that can sometimes happen in medicine, the defence say, in a case like this, there's a danger in an expert being drawn into filling the absence of an explanation with an explanation that is influenced by the prosecution theory that harm has or might have been done. So the expert might be drawn into landing on a harm-based explanation where that may not be the only explanation. You'll see how that's dealt with and whether that is the case when we come to the evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I appreciate it's slightly in a vacuum as I'm describing it now, but it's a bit like if somebody looks for something with something in mind, no matter how they try to get rid of that thought, they may well see that and not see other things. It's an example of what people call confirmation bias sometimes: once you have an idea in your head, you tend to just see the things that fit with that and you either reject or don't even look for other things. That can happen without people realising it's happening or the strength with which it's happening. That's when you are so important in assessing that evidence: if you're aware of this, you're not inside their head, you can assess it overall.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, this case has involved, ladies and gentlemen, the consideration of reports by experts on behalf of the prosecution and the defence and we'll hear from prosecution experts during the prosecution case and if the defence call any expert evidence, that comes as part of the defence case, although you will appreciate there is no burden on the defence to call any expert evidence at all. But the fact is there has been a number of experts who have looked at the situations in this case and, as you'll hear in the evidence, they have been provided with one another's reports before this trial and they've even met as a group and considered their opinions jointly, so they all know what one another is saying. That's quite normal in a situation like this, it helps narrow down where the areas of disagreement are, but there is plenty of disagreement, we say.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So let me set out, ladies and gentlemen, the issues on the medical evidence across the counts on the indictment, and I have to say, as far as simplifications go, this is a big one, but just a couple of words of caution first.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: When I do this, you'll understand, the burden isn't on the defendant to provide an explanation. I'm not saying that as an excuse for anything because we're seeking to do so, you'll see that, but as a matter of law it's not. But in case where we are dealing with complex evidence like this, it is important to keep that in mind because the answers won't always be clear.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Doctors don't always have the answers and nor do medical experts.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So please keep in mind sometimes there may not be an immediate and apparent explanation, and I just say that as a way of caution. The fact, for example, that Ms Letby cannot explain a particular event or that it can't be explained on her behalf does not mean she must be responsible for it. We'll look at all the evidence for that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The second word of caution is this: what I am about to do is done to help you and the court with this complicated part of the evidence. What I'm not doing is to provide a checklist of points for the defence case to be measured against as if this is some sort of game.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You'll appreciate that: we are not playing a game here.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The burden remains always on the prosecution to prove the case. What I'm setting out is a bare summary of the issues. We don't have to do that, but we want to help and we want you naturally to understand important parts of the case and this will be looked at far more closely when we come to the evidence, and you
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: will see there is a good deal of challenge where the evidence is concerned.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: What I'm not going to do each time I come to one of the counts on the indictment, ladies and gentlemen, is remind you that Ms Letby is adamant that she has done nothing intentionally to harm any of these babies. That applies to every count, but it doesn't require me to say it every time we turn to it. It will help you -- you may have it already -- if you can see the indictment just as we turn to this now and have a look at these issues.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So count 1. An allegation of murder in the case of [Baby A]. I'll remind you each time -- again, an absolute bare summary -what the prosecution say. They say this is the result of an air embolus being introduced into a blood vessel, so air of some form.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: A general point, since this is the first time we come to the question of air embolus, air emboli or air emboluses. A general point: the defence accept in this instance, and other cases involving the allegation of air embolus, we accept it is a theoretical possibility.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's the first thing: it's accepted it's something that can happen or could happen. So we're not saying this is an impossibility. But of course, the defence accepting that it is a theoretical possibility doesn't really establish very much since in medicine many things can be a theoretical possibility. Many things could be the case. We don't start convicting people of murder and attempted murder because it could be the case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's important.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The issue is whether in each case the evidence proves what's being said, whether it's sufficient to safely diagnose that it was an air embolus. It's one thing to say, yeah, it could be. But could it? Was it?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: All kinds of things could be.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So the question when we come to this is: does the evidence take us there? What's the basis for it? And then we'll come to questions relating to the practicalities: well, maybe it is, how? Or if it could be, how? I'm not going to go into that every time on these because I am going to assist you by focusing on the medical evidence. Questions of what happened factually on each occasion we'll probably hear or look at in more detail with the witnesses describing what happened. This is just to do with the medical evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So on this count, the defence do not accept that air embolus is the cause of what happened. What we do say is that the care given to [Baby A] at the unit was, to use an expression you have heard before, sub-optimal. This is the polite and legal way of saying below the right standard. It wasn't optimal, it wasn't what it should be -- and plainly not a reference to Lucy Letby when we say that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say that [Baby A] may have collapsed either as a result of a lack of fluids, we'll come to the evidence behind this when we get to the contents of the trial, either as a result of a lack of fluids or a result of the various lines that had been put into him and poorly sited, including the potential for them to interfere with his heart rate.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Now, you will hear, and you may not recall, but you may, that in his case, as in some of the others, air is identified in one or more abdominal vessels after death.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There are radiographs taken where you can sometimes see air.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You will hear in this case that the fact of air on a radiograph after death is not of itself something that automatically goes to prove, for example, an air embolus. Air is produced in the body after death very rapidly and is capable for accounting for air seen on that kind of imaging. It's what's called a postmortem (inaudible: distorted) and it happens quickly. So that will be something to consider. These are real issues.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's not enough to say there's air in the abdominal vessels -that can happen post-mortem. That's [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to turn next to count 2, [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We'll follow these as we go through. The allegation here is that [Baby B]’s airway was blocked in some way or there was an air embolus given to her. The defence say no. She had been in a precarious condition from birth.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Like [Baby A], she had been born at 31 weeks and in her case she was blue and floppy when she was born. We do not accept that the signs she exhibited give any support for diagnosing an air embolus nor is there anything to support an airway being blocked.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say that's a good example of the assumption of guilt: there's been a collapse, there's been some sort of problem, and we say — and you'll assess this -- those involved in looking at it, the prosecution experts, have been influenced by the theory that harm was done and that's influenced the outcome rather than
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: simply looking at it neutrally and concluding that harm was done.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say it's also relevant in [Baby B]’s case that she had other episodes when she struggled to breathe after the time on the indictment here, episodes that don't appear in that table, but there were other episodes when she struggled to breathe, so it's part of an issue that she appeared to display.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 3, ladies and gentlemen, [Baby C]. I'm going to pause just to say this -- and really it's going back to something I said at the outset: I appreciate I am trying to go slowly, but at the same to travel through these. We realise this is people's lives and these are babies and to do with families. Please don't think -- I wouldn't want anyone to think, when I'm going through it like this, we don't appreciate that. That's always the case. So there's nothing meant to be insensitive or heavy-handed in dealing with it in the way I am now, it is just to help you, and I am sure everyone understands this is where the key areas are going to be on the medical evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 3, [Baby C]. The prosecution experts say that in this case death was a consequence of air introduced exogenously, so brought into the stomach, by the nasogastric tube. They're saying that's been done on purpose. We'll see, again, exactly how that is explained when the prosecution experts come to give evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But pausing before I deal with [Baby C]’s case in particular, a general point about those allegations that involve air being said to have been forced down the nasogastric tube. Again, I hope this is reasonable and helps, so we know what we're dealing with. We accept in this case, as in other ones where that's the mechanism alleged, that someone's injected air or forced it or forced something down the tube to cause abdominal distension. We agree that is a theoretical possibility.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not saying it couldn't have happened. It's a theoretical possibility. But that, as you will understand, is a very long way from saying, yes, the evidence proves that's what's taken place. Again, all sorts of things might account for abdominal distension.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It wouldn't be very helpful if we were even disputing something which, as a matter of theory, could account for it. Of course it could. When we come to look at the allegations you will need to look, for example, at the practicalities of that, how this is meant to have been done. This is another matter altogether.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And the question of whether there are alternatives that account for abdominal distension, because abdominal distension, swelling
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: in the stomach and intestinal area and into the bowel, is not uncommon in babies or babies on neonatal units. And you will see reference to it at other times that don't appear on this indictment. The prosecution would say, yes, but they're not as dramatic as this. Well, we'll see and we'll go through all of that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So coming to [Baby C]. He was 30 weeks gestation and 800 grams, so that is very premature and very low birth weight. Connecting that with an issue I've identified earlier about birth condition, as a starting point, sadly, a baby like that will be vulnerable to a variety of complications, what's called respiratory distress syndrome, which is when it's difficult to breathe because, of course, their lungs have not developed. The mere fact of the baby being born doesn't mean that they are going to be at the same (inaudible: coughing) as a baby that is term. That growth is meant to go on. More vulnerable to infection.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And we say, for a starting point, he should have been at a unit delivering more specialist care. He was at the Countess of Chester and we say they did not provide appropriate care and that condition, NEC, that you heard about, the bowel condition, necrotising enterocolitis, or infection, are both potential causes of collapse and death.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We also say it's relevant that the pathology, so after death, identified acute pneumonia with acute lung injury. That was one of the findings. Again, to help, the response from the prosecution, we anticipate, would be, yes, it's one thing to die with pneumonia, that doesn't mean somebody died of it. So to be of help, we point out there's two sides of looking at that, but it may be a relevant finding.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There is also, we say, a question as to whether in the formation of his gut in the abdominal cavity there was a structural blockage that could have caused distension. There are a number of issues there. But when we go back to the cases in detail we'll come back to these and you'll see them then with the evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 4, [Baby D], one of the allegations of air embolus, air into a blood vessel. The defence say, no, we do not accept that air embolism can be properly diagnosed here. We say the hospital failed to provide appropriate care -- and actually this is accepted by the prosecution to some extent, as they said in opening, and as they would have to do, because it's beyond dispute she was not put on antibiotics when she should have been; there was a delay of hours.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In a little baby, that's a big delay. When people talk about -what you'll hear is the golden hour or the time in which various things should be done to look after a neonate, there's a reason why they should be done quickly. In her case there was a delay of hours.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: She was never able to breathe unaided and we say there is strong evidence that infection may have played a part in her death and a good deal stronger than any suggestion of air embolus. And in her case there is clear evidence also of pneumonia after her death. How relevant that is is something we'll consider with the experts, but that's a finding.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And where there is air in her system, seen in it on imaging after death, we say that is potentially due to post-mortem changes or even resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 5, [Baby E]. The allegation here, in fact, is of air embolus and acute gastrointestinal haemorrhage, a lot of bleeding from the stomach area or the intestine area. You will remember, ladies and gentlemen, [Baby E] is the little boy who the prosecution say was attacked by Lucy Letby in front of his own mother.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, we'll come to the evidence on which that is said to be based in due course. We say there is no evidence of an air embolus, no proper evidence, and actually no evidence of direct trauma identified that could account for the blood loss. For all that's said about that, there's no evidence of it, although he did die of acute haemorrhage.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say there is no clear explanation in his case for what happened. But that being so, it is not right to reach or rely upon the assumption of guilt. You may recall this is a case where there was no post-mortem.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The prosecution told you about that and they said that was a big mistake, like somehow there was a problem for them. Well, yes, too right that's a mistake. You may wonder who's paying the price for that now because, in the absence of a post-mortem, the defence will say the prosecution are able and the experts are able to float suggestions as to deliberate harm, the reality of which we do not know.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Counts 6 and 15, ladies and gentlemen. I'm going to deal with those together. You may realise why. That's because they're the two counts that involve allegations of insulin being introduced. Count 6, [Baby F].
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 15, [Baby L].
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The defence cannot say what has happened and, to be fair, it might be observed if someone has done nothing wrong, how could they? It's difficult to say what has happened if you don't know. We say because of that, rather than just not looking at it closely, there is all the more reason to look very closely at the evidence relating to both of these allegations. And we invite that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: From what happened with the bags, the TPN bags that are said to have been hung up with insulin in them, to the point that the samples were taken and the testing, these are hotly disputed, as are the other allegations.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And as with other allegations our concern is the absence of being able to explain things is not converted into evidence of guilty.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But such a lot has been made of this and so much said about poisoning that I am going to pause and identify an issue on the facts just to illustrate that these are not simple allegations that can just be rolled out and automatically lead to a conviction. Far from it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I don't know how much you remember of the description of what happened with the various bags that were put up involving [Baby F]. You'd do well if you can remember it because even though it was gone through in detail, quite properly, it's a little while ago.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Just to remind you, a bag was put up when Lucy Letby was on duty, a little after midnight on 5 August. And there were problems, low blood sugar, some hours later.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That bag was changed some time around midday of the next day when she wasn't there, and the problems continued, even though the bag was changed. And then the sample that was taken and is relied on in this count for the insulin reading came from the second bag, the bag that was put up when she wasn't there, whatever lies behind that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The prosecution say, well, that must have been a random stock bag. So that isn't even anything that was designated for [Baby F]. And yet that found its way to him when she wasn't there and when that simply cannot be blamed on her.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The prosecution are fixed to the theory that this is all to do with Lucy Letby, so in trying to explain how this can have happened, the different bags and different times and when she isn't there, they have the authority on this, Professor Hindmarsh, who you may recall has given not one but three possible explanations for what happened, none of which directly
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: implicate Lucy Letby, and that might leave you thinking, and this is the point, we'll come to it in the evidence, this is a good deal less clear than it sounded when you were first told about insulin poisoning.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We observe it's hardly surprising the prosecution ended up saying, as they did when dealing with this, "It's all a bit of a headache". You may not remember that being said, we would say not surprising, no, but not very reassuring.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: They also said on this topic it's not straightforward and we certainly agree. That doesn't mean we just use the assumption of guilt to make it straightforward.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Two bags, at least, three possibilities, and Lucy Letby not there when the bag was put up from which the sample that was analysed was taken.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So after all of that, the prosecution, we say, hardly surprising, say, let's see how the evidence goes, and with that we agree wholeheartedly. If there's anything we should walk (sic) away from this it's: let's see how the evidence goes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We come to [Baby L]. There are issues there relating to the documentation and the entries and the timing of what happened with the bags and who was involved. So we challenge these allegations too, however much reliance is put on them, and we repeat that there is nothing in fact, after all of that, to establish any act certainly by Lucy Letby that shows her doing what is alleged against her.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: [Baby G], ladies and gentlemen, counts 7, 8 and 9.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The prosecution experts say there are a number of things that happened here. They say there was excessive milk forced down the NGT, the nasogastric tube, on two occasions, counts 7 and 8, and then on count 9 there's the incident when it's said that Lucy Letby was behind a screen with [Baby G] when the doctors had been -- after the doctors had finished fitting a cannula to her and [Baby G] was desaturating.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, [Baby G]. Her starting point was an extremely premature baby, born on what the doctors would describe, it's not meant to be insensitive, but born on the margins of viability. These are all official terms and medical terms as you'll hear. Again you'll know, and you'll be learning, if you didn't know already, that that means there will be problems that you can predict and that will automatically be associated with this.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So experts coming along and say, oh, so-and-so's doing really well -- well, we'll look at that. In any real world sense we
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: say, no, that's not a baseline to start from. She was a highrisk baby with a history of abdominal distension and vomiting, irrespective of anything associated with Lucy Letby, and on occasions that don't feature in any reference that's been made so far in this indictment or that table. We say they all form part of an ongoing and relevant picture.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In addition, the defence say she exhibited signs of infection and so we do not accept that Lucy Letby had anything to do with causing the vomits on counts 7 and 8.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Again, when we get to the evidence you'll be able to see and weigh up what all parties say about what could have happened. These are the things to look out for: a history of vomiting, reflux, things like that, which fit with what we find on the 7th and the 8th. Nor do the defence accept that Ms Letby did anything to cause the desaturation on count 9, and that's a count where we will hear evidence of who was where and who did what and what could possibly have lay behind the moment that Lucy Letby called [Nurse B] to come and help her because [Baby G] was desaturating. She called for help.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Counts 10 and 11, ladies and gentlemen, [Baby H]. You will become increasingly familiar with the situations for each of these little children as we go through the case and then you'll begin to think, yes, this is the case that involves the following things, and of course the person that's behind them.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's all about people.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: [Baby H] is the baby who was treated with three chest drains. I will just remind you that in opening the prosecution said that her case is complicated to a degree by the sub-optimal treatment she received at the beginning of her life. An unacceptable delay in intubating her. An unacceptable delay in giving her surfactant, which is the protein that's put into the lungs to assist with breathing. She wasn't paralysed when put on the ventilator initially. Butterfly needles were left in her chest for prolonged periods of time, which may have punctured her lung.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say, and the prosecution accept this, so far as those things are concerned, first of all, another example of sub-optimal care. And the prosecution experts appear to have no real explanation for what happened. Certainly no specific way is proposed in which she was deliberately harmed. It seems, we observe, that a good deal of harm which was done to her by what happened in the hospital has nothing to do with Lucy Letby, but despite all of that, she's there. And we say that [Baby H]'s collapses were probably the result of infection or the trauma of
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: what happened in the unit and it isn't anything that Lucy Letby did and in fact there is nothing to establish that it was.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 12, ladies and gentlemen, [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: You'll remember when we come to [Baby I]’s case, although the allegation of murder relates to 23 October 2015, on this count we're looking at a series of events, a number of events that happened that the prosecution say were attempts to kill her leading up to that date, three previous events.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Various mechanisms are proposed here by the prosecution experts. There is excessive air into the NGT, air embolus into the blood vessel on different occasions and sometimes together. Dr Dewi Evans, who is an expert for the prosecution, agrees this is a complicated case and we observe most of what we are dealing with in this trial, we would suggest, is fairly complicated. But we say if you follow [Baby I]’s course of health and treatment across her sadly short life you will see that her collapses and ultimately her death are part of a series of ongoing clinical problems that may well have been inevitable given her extreme prematurity. She was 27 weeks old at gestation.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We also say when we are looking at the question of abdominal distension there are times when CPAP may have caused or contributed to that distension. We do not accept that air was forced down the NGT and we do not accept that air embolus is something that happened at all.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I want to pause there for a moment to explain what I mean when I say CPAP may have caused abdominal distension. You have heard this referred to already by the prosecution, it's in the glossary but I will just read it:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "CPAP is continuous positive airway pressure, a method of noninvasive respiratory support, by which air with supplemental and/or oxygen (as necessary) is administered through a face mask or plastic tubes into the nose at a constant pressure to reduce the work of breathing and improve oxygenation in babies."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So by non-invasive, that means it's not the tubes -endotracheal tubes going all the way, like on a ventilator. It's not as, if I put it this way, extreme or invasive as that as. It comes in on a mask or tubes into the nose and of course that means there is a pressure of air entering the baby. And it's a recognised complication of CPAP that it can, in circumstances, cause an expansion or a distension of the abdomen; it's called CPAP belly.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There are measures that can be taken to avoid that or to reduce it, to ensure air is taken out of the baby as the baby is on
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: CPAP and things like that, but whilst it isn't for the defence to provide explanations for everything, we do observe that there are times when CPAP may have caused or contributed to abdominal distension in this case.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 13, ladies and gentlemen, [Baby J]. We say there's not a great deal of explanation here from the prosecution experts as to what caused the deterioration in [Baby J]’s case. Dr Evans has suggested airway obstruction. Well, we'll see, but just to refresh your memories, [Baby J] was the little girl who had the ileostomy performed and was provided surgically with stomas, and those are to enable faeces to pass outside her body. It may be her collapse was due to infection, but what we do say is that the Countess of Chester Hospital was well out of its depth in looking after or attempting to look after [Baby J] and knowing how to treat her.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say that you will see here, or may see, an assumption of deliberate harm combined with Lucy Letby's presence on the unit being used to direct blame at her when what we actually have is a baby receiving inadequate care and a baby for whom there is no mechanism that can be identified that links her collapse to anything that Lucy Letby did.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: [Redacted]. Again, I hope -- (inaudible) all going in, it's a lot to deal with.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We'll take it through like this, hopefully, ladies and gentlemen, bit by bit you'll be able to listen to relevant matters when we get to these counts in the evidence. I'm sure the prosecution will do the same to assist.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: [Redacted]. I am just keeping an eye on the time and the temperature.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If I may, I will continue for the time being, with your Lordship's leave, but, ladies and gentlemen, it may be before I get to the end if what I have to say, that depending on the time, a short break would be of assistance, but could I stop at that point, my Lord, and just check with the court?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Count 16 is next, ladies and gentlemen. We have had a brief look at count 15 as we have had brief looks at the other counts. Count 16, [Baby M]. The allegation is air embolus being introduced or airway obstruction.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The defence recognise there is no obvious cause of collapse in this case. But we certainly don't accept that the evidence
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: establishes an air embolus or any other form of interference. It's just how that is.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There is no obvious thing. We're not pointing to this or pointing to that. No obvious cause. There may be some sign he was developing an infection. Be that as it may, we say we are back in the territory, really, of blame being put on Ms Letby because there is no obvious alternative. That is what I mean (sic) earlier when I was talking about the assumption guilt and the coincidence -- we get to a point in this case where just the mere fact she is there when something has happened is almost being used as an explanation for it happening.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Counts 17 to 19, ladies and gentlemen, are relating to [Baby N]. On 3 June the allegation is there was some kind of inflicted trauma, so something done to him physically that caused him to scream or air was being injected. On 15 June, it's alleged that bleeding was caused by an NGT being pushed into his throat. You'll remember the things the prosecution have said about [Baby N] and the diagnosis that he was or may be a haemophiliac and therefore they say maybe that's what lies behind this.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, as for 3 June, which is count 17, the defence observe there are many reasons why a baby will shout or scream. Their being hurt is one of them but in fact on a neonatal unit not the most obvious, unless you are going to assume that someone's done it. We say it is far more likely to be hunger, and that might sound banal, it might sound a bit obvious or simple. Well, sometimes things can be. You certainly won't find evidence of anything else and no basis for injected air.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's 3 June. 15 June, counts 18 and 19. In particular I'm going to concentrate on count 18, in the morning, the allegation that Lucy Letby did something that caused him to bleed in his throat.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Just to remind you, it was at about 8 o'clock that morning when [Dr A] had to intubate [Baby N] and what the prosecution say is that when he came to do that, he saw blood already in [Baby N]'s throat. So the allegation is, well, something had been done to [Baby N] to make him bleed. And that's the prosecution case on that, and because [Baby N] was with Lucy Letby, or she could have been with him, she had done something to do it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The defence disagree. We are going to have to look carefully at the medical notes here. We disagree that Lucy Letby harmed him then, or at any time that day, and in fact the only fair and reasonable interpretation of the notes and what happened is that blood was not identified until intubation had happened or was part-way through. There were three attempts to intubate him by [Dr A] and the defence say squarely that there was blood by the
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: end of that, but there is no basis for saying there was blood before it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say also in [Baby N]'s case there was sub-optimal care and he is another child who should have been at a tertiary unit and not at the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I am coming to the last three here, ladies and gentlemen. That's not to diminish their importance.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'm grateful for the focus, it's a lot to take in in detail like this.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 20, [Baby O], also known as [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The allegations here are various. What is proposed is intravenous air embolus, so air into the bloodstream, trauma being done to the liver, so some sort of attack or impact into the area of the liver, and excessive air into the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The defence do not accept any of those three mechanisms proposed by the prosecution experts and we say they are not the only possible explanations. The question of discolouration, which is used to support air embolus -- and you'll remember -- you'll hear, I imagine, a lot about this in evidence from the experts, so here's something to identify, the way that the changes in colour on a baby's skin are said to indicate an air embolus having been injected. That's what that comes down to, whether or not that can be used to identify an air embolus, whether it's good enough to be used for anything diagnostically, there's this question of the strange mottling or the colour of children who have an air embolus. We do not accept anything approaching that is established on this count.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We also say there were signs of infection in [Baby O] and that could have played a part in his collapse.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We also say this: that a rapid rate in the increase -- or rather the rate of increase in his feeding at this time, together with the respiratory support he was receiving -- you heard me talk about CPAP, CPAP belly -- those combined will have increased the pressure in his abdomen and the extent of the distension, and the distension is caused or can be caused by that, rather than air forced down the NGT.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Again, you will understand at this point we're just focusing on the bare medical evidence. You will have the advantage of taking the medical evidence and also listening to evidence from doctors or nurses who were there where that's available and what they describe what happened so then you can think, well, what are the
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: practicalities of this, what might or might not have happened or, rather, when we're dealing with serious criminal allegations, what are we sure has happened.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So far as the injury to [Baby O]’s liver is concerned, the defence say that is in fact something that could have been caused during resuscitation. The prosecution do not accept that. I have not been saying every time the prosecution do not accept that, but I'm sure you follow, ladies and gentlemen, the prosecution say one thing and often the defence do not accept that. The defence say something, often the prosecution do not accept that. But it would be very tedious if I kept on saying they don't accept it every time.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Again in [Baby O]’s case we say that where air was identified on radiographs post-mortem that is a natural occurrence that happens after death.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 21, [Baby P]. It is another allegation of excessive air into the stomach, which, as we have heard, splints the diaphragm, so holds it hard, and then the baby can't breathe and then collapse follows. That's the allegation. The defence agree that collapse can occur, or could have occurred here, by splinting of the diaphragm but we don't agree with the way that it is alleged to have happened.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say that the air that was identified in [Baby P]’s stomach and intestine is consistent with the build-up of air from something called Optiflow, which no doubt I'll be corrected eventually, but for the purposes of this is a bit like CPAP, it's air going into the baby for respiratory support, and that was blowing into the nasopharynx area for hours. That's this area here (indicating) that goes down into the throat area, towards the chest area.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Again, in his case, that was happening at the same time as a rapid advancement in the rate of his feeding.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That can account for the dilation. And in his case, ladies and gentlemen -- and this is something, an issue to identify, keep in mind -- there was a significant degree of distension in [Baby P]’s case, almost, it seems, the entire bowel from the stomach to the rectum. And there's an issue, isn't there, as to how long would that take for somebody to inflict that? That's one of the examples of what we mean by what are the practicalities?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's one thing to say, well, we're not sure what it is, but she was there and harm has been going on, so she did it. Well, how?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: On the other hand, it's entirely possible for a baby in this situation, who's on CPAP or Optiflow over a period of time, for
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: air to build up in that way if it isn't being aspirated or drained in some other way.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We agree that once he collapsed it is not clear why he didn't respond to resuscitation, but that doesn't go to show that this is inflicted harm. Just so you can follow what's said.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There may be an issue in his case, let's put it this way for the time being, as to whether the amount of adrenaline given to him during the collapse might actually have contributed to that deterioration and made it worse.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Count 22, [Baby Q]. It's the last count on this indictment. Air injected via the nasogastric tube and possibly a fluid of some sort being given to him as well. This might be a little fresher in your recollection because we listened to this described by the prosecution this morning.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Again, the defence do not accept this and we say that in the days prior to his collapse, [Baby Q] had actually developed bile-stained aspirate, so what was being drawn out of his stomach area is stained by bile.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That shouldn't be there. We say that indicates a problem with his bowel and is capable of supporting a diagnosis of NEC -remember the gut complaint, quite a serious one, that can occur in small children and babies -- and that a poorly functioning bowel is probably what led to him being unwell and vomiting on 25 June.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And yes, gas was aspirated from his stomach, but again he had been receiving what's called positive pressure ventilation. You can't possibly say the gas wasn't from that, it was from an assault of some sort.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So ladies and gentlemen, you will see -- that is a simple -- to say it's a simple summary is no overstatement, it really is a simple summary of what we are dealing with. You will see there are real issues to be considered but the purpose for going through it that way, and I'm grateful for you for (inaudible: distorted) to that is that so you understand the type of issues
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: we're looking at and the sort of things to look for.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There are two areas I'd like to deal with before I conclude.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: My Lord, if we were to break, this would be the point, but I don't want to delay things unnecessarily.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It will probably take me about 20-25 minutes just to finish this.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I think in the circumstances, we will have a short break. We're going to have a break, the question is whether we have one now or in 20 or 25 minutes when this is finished because we're going to have to have a break to deal with you continuing as a jury of 14 in any event. Are you happy to wait until then? Wait until then?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Very well.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: (Pause)
The fourth area. Looking now at Ms Letby and the question of her presence at the relevant time and what the evidence can establish about what she was doing.

These are far more general comments than the earlier part of what I have said to you, so I'm not going through, on this count did this and on that count did that, but these are the sort of things we can keep in mind generally and then look at the evidence.

When we come to the question of where Ms Letby was and what she was doing, nothing is meant to sound sinister in saying that. It's just a simple question: where was she, what was she doing? I need hardly say, it's important not to guess or, even worse, proceed on an assumption of guilt. It's important to keep this in mind because a lot of the time you're going to find the evidence cannot pinpoint exactly where she was any more than it can pinpoint exactly where another person was.
Even where we have timings on certain documents, they will not always be precise timings of what we're dealing with. Some will be more precise than others.
She can certainly hardly be expected to remember.

How on earth, outside notes that are made at the time, is anyone going to remember. But of course that makes it all too easy for someone to say she could have been attacking a child. That is in fact what we get over and over again, we say.

When you come to look at the relevant detail in these events, in particular when we look at particular problems as they develop, we say there are many occasions when Lucy Letby was simply not there at the time she would have had to be present if she'd been doing the type of deliberate harm alleged. And it would be very unfair to say she is responsible because she's there and enters the scene when the course has already been set.
Sometimes there are relevant events that take place when she's nowhere near to what's happening and we say some events like that don't make it on to that table.

Now, to assist, so you have both sides of this issue in mind, we acknowledge the prosecution may say, or will say, yeah, but the events on that table are the relevant events, they're the ones that matter for these children.
They may say other things are not as dramatic or serious or unexplained, it's these ones that stand out.

The defence are saying, no, there are other ones we need to look at to put these in context, and deciding that is part of what will be involved in that trial, but then you have both sides of that issue, ladies and gentlemen, and it's something to consider as we go along. I've endeavoured to put both sides of it there so you can see what the competing arguments are.

Even when Ms Letby is present, even when there is no dispute that she is looking after one of these children at the time of one of these events, really that does not get anywhere close to proving what the prosecution allege.

And disregarding how unfair it would be just to treat mere presence as evidence of guilt -- and we are going to submit to you that's where this gets to very much -- you'll need to keep this in mind. This is something to look at when you come to the evidence, something to be considered in the questioning of how events or shifts were arranged on the unit. She was a young nurse with no immediate family commitment and, the defence say, someone who built her life around her work in the neonatal unit. She obtained the qualifications, both to do that and to be able to deliver intensive care because, sadly, a number of children there labour under serious health problems.

So, we say, she was often called in to cover shifts where there were babies with those sort of difficulties and sometimes at short notice and she was ready to do so. So it follows that someone in that position and that role is more likely to be looking after the more clinically difficult babies and be more likely to be there when deteriorations happen and that doesn't mean she made it happen.

Finally, on the subject of Ms Letby and her presence and what did happen or what didn't happen, it's important, isn't it, to bear in mind that she will, perhaps often, not be able to remember all the details relating to specific children and particular events?

I'm saying that now because of course you have heard things that were said in interviews, you have heard summaries of that, and we'll come to the interviews in due course. But just keep that in mind, that in that regard she's like any other witness in this case whose recollection often cannot go beyond the notes made at the time. You'll weigh this up when you hear what's said.

Although you may find some examples of prosecution witnesses whose memories have improved over time, we'll see. Look out for that. Goodness knows how many babies she will have cared for over the years. Keep in mind she cannot be expected to remember details better than any other witness. And sometimes it may be impossible for her to say what she was doing when there are no records to help. I should think it must be uncontroversial to say that would make her guilty of nothing. Look out for the way that any difficulties she has in recollection is in any way used against her.

And the fifth and the final area that I'm going to deal with in this outline of the facts, ladies and gentlemen, or rather outline of the issues, is the issue relating to other staff and the unit as a whole.

That must be important, mustn't it? It must be because it would be unbalanced and unfair to focus on Lucy Letby's role with a particular child if there are associated and potentially relevant problems created by others or in the way the unit was run. That may explain or may go some way towards explaining what happened.
This is one of the things we've identified that doesn't appear on the prosecution's chart. Why would it? It's not a part of that exercise.

Now, nobody -- nobody -- is going to expect perfection day in, day out. What is expected in terms of care from medical practitioners is generally not to make things worse. And can I make it plain, we do not suggest that the doctors and the nurses on this unit were anything other than dedicated to doing the best they could and the work they do is admirable and crucial. But if this is going to be fair, if we're going to weigh this up fairly, you may think it is important to consider whether any problems in practice or in the way the unit was staffed and run could have contributed to what we have on this indictment unless we're simply not interested in finding out what's happened, we're just going to say, oh well, we don't really care about that, it's just the coincidence when she was there. You may agree, that would be desperately unfair.

What I'm saying is not fanciful. We say there were problems with the way this unit performed that had nothing to do with Lucy Letby and we will look closely at this in evidence. I'm not going to go through a list of things now.

But you may have sensed, as we've reminded you, an element of it and one or two concessions in the protection opening. The failure to give antibiotics to [Baby D] is a legitimate target of criticism, although Lucy Letby is held responsible for her death on count 4.
The fact that the care of [Baby H] was sub-optimal repeatedly, although Lucy Letby is held responsible for the collapses on counts 10 and 11.

The defence say there are very many more examples of sub-optimal performance in this unit that are also legitimate targets of criticism. We will come to that in the evidence and then you can weigh up what I'm suggesting and identifying for you now.

Included in this area is the way in which a significant number of children in this case recovered well, or better, when they were moved from the Countess of Chester Hospital. Repeatedly, the prosecution have said how much better certain babies did when they were moved to a tertiary unit, like Arrowe Park Hospital or Liverpool Women's Hospital, and the prosecution consistently put that down to the fact that they had been moved away from Lucy Letby. You've heard that repeatedly.

Of course, an equal and alternative and equally viable interpretation is that their improvement coincided with removal from the Countess of Chester Hospital, which could not deliver, we say, on all occasions the care that was necessary or the expertise for some of the children it looked after.

We say that the improvement in some of these children when they went to a tertiary unit is evidence of how the unit at the Countess of Chester did not always deliver the care at the level it should have been provided. To turn that round and put it all back on to Lucy Letby, is unfair and inaccurate.

You may recall, during the period on the indictment, that the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester was what's called a level 2 unit. I'm going to deal with this because this is an important aspect of this part of the case.
You'll hear there are three levels of unit in neonatal care. Level 1 is the -- I think this is a simplification again -- the least intensive care.
Level 3 offers the highest level of intensive care.
That's called the tertiary unit, that's the highest level, the most specialist. So units like Arrowe Park and Liverpool Women's Hospital are level 3 or tertiary, they specialise in the highest level.

As a level 2 unit, so that's, you might think, in the middle, it can provide some degree of intensive care, the Countess of Chester could offer care to babies from 27 weeks gestation if they were what's called single births and 28 weeks for multiple births. So if a baby's gestation is lower than that, he or she should go to a tertiary, they shouldn't be at a secondary like Countess of Chester.

We say there are occasions when the level of care at this unit could not reach the level of care required for the babies it was caring for, whether that is because of a lack of technical medical skill on behalf of doctors or because it was accepting babies with too high a care requirement for its capacity, or simply because it was too busy because and could not deliver what was required with the staff it had available. I'm identifying this now, ladies and gentlemen, so you are able to listen out for evidence relating to this if it emerges during the course of the trial.

It's an issue we say that will feature in the evidence so I'm identifying it for that reason. You will learn, when we get to the evidence, that in July 2016, shortly after Ms Letby had been moved to non-clinical duties, the Countess of Chester neonatal unit was redesignated to a level 1. So in effect, the seriousness of the cases it could deal with was reduced.

I'm sure there are more formal bureaucratic expressions for that. I'm not going to use the expression "downgraded" because every level of care is important, but, you can follow, they could no longer provide care for babies at the level they did, they could provide level of care for babies of 32 weeks and up. That's what you get with level 1.

You can imagine, in a situation like that, there is bound to be concern -- just imagine the reality of that in a hospital unit — and an inquiry into what has happened. Its redesignation, it's not fair to call it a downgrading, but you can imagine how some people might feel that's what has happened, senior people, people involved with the managing of it, and that may form part of the relevant background in this case, which is almost certainly going to be featuring in the evidence and we say you need to be aware of that.
And in a similar vein, in terms of the relationship between Lucy Letby and the unit where she worked, something else the

prosecution touched on rather coyly was Dr Jayaram and his suspicions. We cannot leave that hanging in this introduction and we want to assist by identifying this. This came up, you'll remember, when we were dealing with [redacted].

You may wonder what on earth that is about because if the prosecution are really saying that Ravi Jayaram, one of the lead consultants on the unit, has suspicions about Lucy Letby, when did that start? Under what basis, you may want to ask? An inquiry like this, looking at everything? You may think that if one or more consultants had suspicions like that, if Lucy Letby was allowed to continue, that's concerning, to put it lightly, if that's what they think. You may wonder whether there's any real basis for suspicion at all and (inaudible: coughing) what Dr Jayaram is talking about when he says that.

You may also think, and this is something to consider when we come to the evidence, that if we're talking about suspicions like that, one or more senior consultants, for example, deciding Lucy Letby is to blame before any formal outside agency is brought in, that that really is fertile, self-serving territory for an assumption of guilt to take hold, and once it does, it affects, we say, the way people look at what is happening, whether they realise it or not. However genuine they are in that belief, it becomes self-serving and self-fulfilling, and often other potentially relevant factors are disregarded.

I'll leave this for the evidence but these are things that have been raised by the prosecution and we cannot move on without dealing with that. For her part Miss Letby would say that, yes, she became in due course a target of blame and wrongly so. So against that background, concluding the redesignation of the unit from a level 2 to a level 1, you may want to ask whether the doctors -- this isn't meant to be some unreasonable assault on everybody, we're not saying it's happening all the time, but whether there are relevant instances in this case where doctors have not given the right care, whether the unit was too busy, whether other members of staff did exactly what was required at key times, and whether they identified all the problems that were emerging at an early enough stage to prevent more serious deterioration. That matters, you will understand, ladies and gentlemen, for three reasons.

First, we say it would be very unfair to judge Lucy Letby by standards that are different or higher than those we are going to apply in this case to other staff at that unit. It would be most unfair to regard something, something she's done or something she's failed to do, something she wrote, something she failed to write, as evidence of murder in her case if it's treated as just one of those things that happen when you come to see how others go about what they do. And that applies not only

to nursing practice but to other areas of evidence, such as the way in which she messages her friends and colleagues, or the timing of that or the interest she shows in families of children she's cared for.
So please don't judge her when we come to the evidence against standards or expectations that are different from those that apply to other nurses on the unit.

Secondly, and more fundamentally, if others have failed to provide appropriate care or if the unit is too busy or not properly staffed, you may agree that creates a situation in which things can go wrong, developing problems may be missed, treatment hurried, mistakes made and records not kept as they should be. They may not always go wrong immediately, but it may happen.

So we must be careful when we turn to the evidence not to hold Lucy Letby responsible if it suggests we are looking at circumstances or outcomes that may not be of her making, whether she's there or not at the time it happens.

And third, keeping in mind what Ms Letby says about the question of blame in her defence, we identify this: that if this unit has failed in such a way that that failing in care has caused or contributed to this uncharacteristic spike in deaths during June 2015 to June 2016, you can imagine pressures to find an explanation. We say the inclination to favour an explanation that distances the unit or those who are directly responsible for running it from blame is quite natural.

Given the scale of what we're dealing with here, the defence say that this may be fertile territory for unconscious bias or for an assumption of guilt to become increasingly attractive. So we say, in conclusion, that is something to keep in mind, isn't it, if we're going to be fair here, as I know you will be, when dealing with what the defence say must be a massive failure in care in a busy hospital neonatal unit and what the defence say is far too great a readiness to lay blame on one person.

Ladies and gentlemen, that really is a brief introduction to the defence case. This whole case is a complex case. It's not straightforward and in that dock is a young woman who says this is not her fault.
So we need to look at the evidence and that's something that we'll be turning to shortly.
