blocks.text: So what we will do now, you'll have your break, but then you're going to come back into court again and be a jury of 12, and I will give you some further jury instructions at that particular point. All right? So it should only take 10 minutes, I think, I'm looking at the usher now. About 10 minutes, yes. Thank you very much. We'll be ready for you when you're ready.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)

Mr Johnson, I'm just wondering about the appropriateness of the iPad instructions this afternoon or whether that should be deferred until tomorrow morning. I don't know, are you confident it can be done in 20 minutes?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's not my confidence that matters, my Lord, it's Mr Murphy's, I think. One way of doing it would be to do the lawyers now and the jury in the morning if your Lordship's worried about their...
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm just thinking at the end of the day, they've had a lot of information today.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Some may be tech savvy, some may not be so tech savvy. We also have some other issues to discuss that we can deal with, so I think what we will do is when the jury comes back into court as a jury of 12, I will just address a few remarks to them and then send them away to come back for 10.30 tomorrow morning.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I agree, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much, Mr Myers. Good.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's what we'll do then.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We'll touch on other matters that need to be addressed insofar as we can, or perhaps at least indicate what can and can't be done and perhaps come back to it tomorrow as well. All right, thank you very much indeed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So this is only going to be about 10 minutes, this break. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (A short break)
(In the presence of the jury)

Right, members of the jury, you are now the jury for the rest of this trial. You, madam, your materials have been moved to the desk that you are now at, so you should have everything, but it's worth just checking that you do have everything in due course, any notes that you may have made. Good, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Time has moved on a bit and we're now at the stage where the next thing that will happen, as far as you're concerned, is you will receive a demonstration on the use of the iPad. That's not going to happen this afternoon, it's going to happen first thing tomorrow morning because I have to deal with some other things and I don't want to send you away -- keep you waiting and call you back in at 4.10 or something like that. So I'm going to -it's been quite a long day for you -- send you away now and, fresh tomorrow morning, you'll have an introduction to the iPad which it is thought will take a maximum of half an hour. Some of you may be very good on iPads already, others of you may not, but it doesn't matter. As Mr Johnson said, you will become very familiar with how to use them and what you can and can't do on them.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: But they are iPads -- I'll tell you now and if I'm wrong in this I'll be corrected tomorrow -- they are simply devices which will have the material in this case on it and nothing else, so you will not be able to access any other source via this iPad.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Each of you will have a personal passcode to it, so you cannot use anyone else's iPad and no one can use your iPad, and you will leave them here, just as you leave any notes here, at the end of the day and they will be here waiting for you the next day and they will be charged overnight. So that's what will happen to them, so they'll all be charged when you're using them and you will be able to make notes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That will all be explained to you, how you can use them -interactive devices, is that the correct expression? So what you can and can't do with them.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Just finally I'm going to come back to those -- remember I gave you my typed directions as well as the note about your responsibilities as a juror? You are now the jury of 12. The situation has now been reached, therefore, that when you are all together as a group of 12, for example if you're sitting outside waiting to come into court, but you're in a private place where other people can't hear what you're saying, apart from the other 11 of you, you may talk about the case to each other. But please do it so that everyone can hear what's being said, so if someone's expressing a view, making a comment or raising something, then the others can hear, unless it's a matter relating to the integrity to you as jurors. In other words, if one of you says, "I'm really worried because something has been said by one of the jurors that shouldn't have been said", you wouldn't discuss that. I told you what you would do when that happens: you instantly bring it to my attention and you don't sit and chat about it as a group of jurors. All right? So that's the situation.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: But the other main rules still remain: you must not talk to anyone else, apart from a fellow juror in the presence of all jurors, about this case, particularly friends and family members. Don't communicate in any way -- don't message, send text messages, do anything like that -- to anyone about anything to do with this case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Do not conduct any research about this case or anything to do with this case. If you read media reports -- and there have been a lot of media reports, as I anticipated there would be -remember it's very selective. You'll have realised that if you've read any of the media reports. The reporters pick certain things out. What they think is important is irrelevant, it's what you think is important. All right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So thank you very much. 10.30 tomorrow morning then as far as you're concerned.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
Further housekeeping
I don't know whether anyone wants to say anything about any other matters before we deal with these -have we got time to deal with this now?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I believe so if you'd like to deal with them, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Are you happy?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, if it's convenient for the court, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The matter that was brought to the court's attention that I brought to your attention. Is there anything anyone wants to say at this stage?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I don't think so immediately. The information I've received, which corresponds to some Google research I did whilst Mr Myers was talking, is that the website is in India, as it happens. That may just be -- as your Lordship's told the jury, information on the internet is not always reliable.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think that's being generous.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, quite.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: A lot of information on the internet is very unreliable and indeed this is unreliable information as well.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There we are. I don't think there's anything we can do. If anyone has any ideas... I'm not proposing to say to the jury, "You should be particularly careful because there's some misreporting", because it will just incite their curiosity.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We'd agree, my Lord. The important thing is the jury have been directed not to look for material and it may be from time to time, I anticipate, if there's going to be a break or something like that, your Lordship probably would remind them not to look at material, but certainly we don't suggest that this should trigger a specific direction because that's almost bound to draw attention to it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I do keep reminding them. I will only be doing it once a day. It will probably come to the stage when I do it once a week almost, but I keep doing it because we're told to keep doing it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. Until events prove otherwise, we have to work on the basis that, quite properly, they'll follow the directions they receive and therefore there's no reason why anybody should be encountering that website and it's not something that would ordinarily -- you would expect it would come to their attention anyway unless someone was looking for it, which they shouldn't be.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We all have to proceed on the basis that, in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the jury are following their instructions. That is a mantra often repeated by the Court of Appeal.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, I've heard that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right. Now, Mr Johnson, am I going to be privy to this or is it just going to be for you?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think the position is that your Lordship's offered a bespoke service, if you want it.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'll probably be slower than anybody else.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Would it be more convenient -- I don't want to trivialise this in any way whatsoever. Would it be better if I had mine at 10 o'clock tomorrow morning?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Maybe, and then your Lordship can in effect supervise the jury's version of it.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's what I was wondering.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, from the position of greater knowledge than theirs.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. In those circumstances, what about the defendant? She'll just get the same as the jury?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do you understand that, Ms Letby? When it comes to the demonstration about using the iPad, you will hear what the jury are instructed to do and will you follow it as well? And if you then find you have any difficulty in relation to it,
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: you can communicate in due course with your solicitor and the matter can be taken further, so that you're able to follow it just as much as anyone else.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There was one other matter in relation to the request from one of the media organisations, I think -- is it the BBC? Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, it's a note that's been displayed in the course of the speeches. It hasn't yet been displayed in evidence, but starting with the end point of the inquiry. Inevitably or naturally, we would shy away from greater publication of it. That's a reaction to that. In answer to the request as to whether they would be entitled to have it once, we would say in particular, it's been in evidence, that's entirely a matter for your Lordship.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There are cases where it's in the nature of evidence, for example video evidence, that other witnesses who are yet to give evidence might be affected by that. One might argue there are good reasons for it not to go beyond the court until those witnesses have given evidence. Save for the instinctive caution of defence counsel when faced with the prospect of a greater dissemination of a piece of evidence like that, save for that, I can't, at this point, point to any particular issue that could arise from it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I can't, so notwithstanding our caution at the prospect of it ultimately being published, there's nothing we can say that says it cannot be.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Nothing we can foresee that prevents it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's been quite extensively referred to, not in its entirety but a lot of it has been referred to, and they can report a lot of the phrases that appear in it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But it's a -- well, I won't comment on it as a document, but it's not actually easy to quite piece it all together. I think one can if you have time to study it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mr Johnson, do you have any observations?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No. Clearly, it's a case of intense public interest and the piece of evidence is an important piece of evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's an important piece of objective evidence. It is what it is.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And I can't see how any witness is going to be prejudiced --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- or therefore the administration of justice is going to be prejudiced by its publication.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. In those circumstances you may publish it. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Can I raise the issue of the initials, the letter that your Lordship received this morning?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Certainly, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: To adopt a different system now to the one we've --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I understand what you're saying. It would be difficult to change it. But why is that exactly?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm not quite sure I understand why someone who was JE and it becomes number 3...
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: A host of -- well, it introduces for all of us a conceptual level of complexity to an already very complex case that on the face of it -- if there is justification for it, then of course we'll have to get on with it. One of the problems is that we have -- there are two documents, in a loose term, or compilation of documents. One is the sequence of events. I don't know if your Lordship's actually seen it.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You gave me two examples, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So we have that, which concentrates on the medical records of a specific child, so each of the children named on the indictment. What we also have is what's been termed the neonatal review or the neonatal unit review. That concentrates on events in the unit that surround the events that the
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: prosecution say in respect of an individual child are significant. So taking as a --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Are you saying that documents would have to be changed?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And a lot?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And a lot. If it's done in a rush, it's likely to cause havoc, and it could actually hold up the trial.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The basic point, my Lord, is that the issue that is being raised in the letter actually is an issue -- it's making the point that people who already know about something are having what they already know confirmed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I know.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's not alerting the wider public. So if parents have already told people about the position of their child, in other words if they've decided not to insist on confidence, they now want to row back from that by in some way making this trial more complicated, and we would submit that that's just not justified, however well-intentioned the solicitor's letter may be.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think what I'm going to do at the moment is I shall invite the court office to respond to -- and there are contact details here?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Speak to the solicitor in question to explain the situation and to invite him, if he wishes to, to come to court and explain in more detail the justification for this because of the points that you raised that it's going to require a considerable -- there's no right to anonymity as such.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, exactly, that's the point, and I can imagine that -- well, anyway.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, no, it's all right. The point is there. It's all right, I understand. Then just say come along and we can probably solve it that way.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In a sense that does not appear to uncaring in relation to the issue.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We're all intensely sympathetic, but there comes a stage at which taking individuals who are not directly affected by the litigation's sensibilities into account makes the litigation itself that much more unmanageable.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And the specific request is to amend the reporting restrictions.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We can't do that.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All your Lordship could do in effect would be to make a case management --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I could make a polite request that they could just report "another baby" rather than giving the initials. But that's, as I would see it, as high as I can go. All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Enquiries are going to be made. Apparently there was someone here from the solicitor's firm this morning in the overflow court. We'll deal with it, but at the moment I'm not going to do or say anything because we're not going to get to that for a time yet, are we?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All right. Thank you all very much, anything else?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No? Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So as far as the court is concerned, it's sitting at 10.30 tomorrow. Officers, dock officers, just to confirm, the court is sitting at 10.30, so the fact that I'm doing something else at 10 o'clock doesn't matter.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: 10.30 is the sitting of the court. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The court adjourned until 10.30 am on Friday, 14 October 2022)
